Ralph Connor prefaces this foothill tale with a measure of a man's power to help his brother. That measure, he writes, is the love in his heart and his faith that good will win at last. With such love, seeking not its own, and such faith gripping the heart of things, a man may meet many fortunes, but not defeat. The story follows the people of the Foothill Country.

Those men left homes of comfort, often of luxury, for adventurous spirit and open ground. A sky pilot, a minister to the hills, becomes their center. Connor writes of rough camps made gentler by faith and friendship. Hard country, hard men, and a preacher who earns his hearing: that is Connor's foothill gospel in one line.
3257-new-thought-pastels:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox published these New Thought pastels in 1906 with Elizabeth Towne of Holyoke, Massachusetts. The index reads like a creed in miniature: a dialogue, the weed, strength, affirm, the chosen, and the nameless. The word, assistance, credulity, and consciousness follow, with the structure, our souls, the law, and knowledge.

Give, perfection, fear, and the way continue the sequence, toward understood and his mansion. Wilcox writes short, plain verses for readers of the new thought movement, which taught mind over circumstance. Small poems for daily pondering, confident that thought shapes life: the new thought creed in miniature.
326-steep-trails:
John Muir gathers twenty-four field pieces in this volume, written across nearly thirty years of western travel. The sketches first ran as letters and short articles, then were set in order by place and date. They range from California and Utah to Nevada, Oregon, Washington, and the Grand Canyon.

Muir walks Mount Shasta, bathes in Salt Lake, notes Mormon lilies, and climbs Mount Rainier in vivid, close detail. He watches forests, farms, dead mining towns, and river country with a naturalist's care. The book keeps the fresh feel of notes made on the trail, and it shows why Muir became a voice for wild land.
3428-the-two-vanrevels:
Booth Tarkington sets this novel in an Indiana town where two young lives cross after long separation. One figure is a girl leaving years of strict enclosure within the walls and still gardens of a convent school, for whom the bright world outside flashes like a mystery. Around her gather town families, a firm named Gray and Vanrevel, and the social rules of a growing river town.

The story follows courtship, family pride, and a young man's effort to prove himself in business and love. Tarkington writes the town itself as a character, with its serenades, cupola rooms, and June evenings. Readers who enjoy American town novels will find romance, rivalry, and a careful picture of manners in the mid nineteenth century.
3697-a-century-of-roundels:
Algernon Charles Swinburne writes a hundred roundels in this volume, second edition 1883, dedicated to Christina Rossetti. The roundel, a short French form Swinburne loved, runs eleven lines with a refrain repeated from its opening. Contents include Death and Birth, Birth and Death, A Ninth Birthday, and dozens of brief lyrics on love, time, and nature.

Swinburne's dedication says songs light as these may sound, though deep and strong the heart spoke through them, and he hopes they please ears tuned to finer music. The poems favor music over argument, with rhyme and refrain carrying feeling. The book suits readers who enjoy formal lyric poetry and Swinburne's mastery of sound.
4056-two-festivals:
A children's book of festivals opens on the evening before May Day, as boys look forward to a May festival with neighborhood children. Mrs. Chilton reads aloud Milton's lines on the bright morning star, dancing from the east with the flowery May.

Other pieces follow a birthday and a true story, in the same fireside manner as the author's travel tales. The book mixes verse, story, and holiday custom for young readers. Families who like old-fashioned seasonal reading will enjoy short pieces meant to be shared aloud at festival time.
4320-an-enquiry-concerning-the-principle:
David Hume published this enquiry as his mature statement of moral philosophy, and the present text follows a 1912 reprint of the 1777 edition. Hume asks what makes actions good or bad, and he answers by looking at human feeling and usefulness rather than at abstract reason alone. Justice, benevolence, and the social virtues take center stage.

The enquiry is short, clear, and arranged in sections with appendices, including a discussion of justice and its place among the virtues. Hume kept the original spellings, such as connexion and labour, in this reprint. It remains a standard entry point for readers new to Hume, and to the question of where morals come from.
446-a-book-of-remarkable-criminals:
H. B. Irving profiles notorious killers and swindlers in this study of crime and motive. Charles Peace, Robert Butler, Derues, Dr. Castaing, Professor Webster, and the mysterious Mr. Holmes each get a full career, trial, and fall. Partners in crime, from the widow Gras to Eyraud and Bompard, close the set.

Irving writes as a lawyer and historian, weighing evidence, motive, and the law's slow net. He stresses how passion, greed, and pride tangle men in their own deeds. The book reads as both true crime and moral study, careful with facts and keen on why ordinary folk turn to murder.
4546-memoirs-of-the-union-s-three-great-:
Three famous Civil War memoirs stand together in this volume: the personal memoirs of Ulysses S. Grant, William T. Sherman, and Philip H. Sheridan. Grant opens his own account by saying friends often urged him to write, and he had long refused. Near sixty-two, a fall confined him to the house, a business partner failed, and falling securities threatened his income, turning study into a welcome pastime.

Each general tells his war in his own voice, from early life and West Point through Mexican War service to the great campaigns of the 1860s. Together they give a Union commander's view of strategy, hardship, and politics, with the plain detail only a participant could supply. Readers get three classic American war memoirs in one file, best read as history told by the men who made it.
4682-nonsense-novels:
Stephen Leacock gathers ten parodies in Nonsense Novels, offering the book to the public without apology. His contents run from Maddened by Mystery, or The Defective Detective, and Q, a psychic pstory of the psupernatural. They go on to Guido the Gimlet of Ghent, a romance of chivalry, and Gertrude the Governess, or Simple Seventeen. A hero in homespun follows, with the life struggle of Hezekiah Hayloft.

Later parodies include Sorrows of a Super Soul, or The Memoirs of Marie Mushenough, Hannah of the Highlands, and Soaked in Seaweed, or Upset in the Ocean, an old-fashioned sea story. Caroline's Christmas, or The Inexplicable Infant, and The Man in Asbestos, an allegory of the future, close the set. Leacock mocks detective tales, romances, and sea yarns with glee. Readers get a short, funny book, best read when the originals it teases are fresh in mind.
4735-the-shepherd-of-the-hills:
Harold Bell Wright published The Shepherd of the Hills in 1907, dedicating it to Frances, his wife, in memory of a summer in the Ozark hills. They followed an old trail around the rise of Mutton Hollow, nobody knows how old, and from Sammy's lookout watched the day go over western ridges. A Troilus and Cressida passage stands at the head.

Contents open with a stranger, Sammy Lane, and a voice from out the mists. A chat with Aunt Mollie and a chapter called Jest Nobody follow. The story, what is love, and why ain't we got no folks follow. Sammy Lane's folks, a feat of strength, Ollie Stewart's good-by, and the shepherd and his flock come next. Sammy Lane's ambition, the common yeller kind, and a party at Ford's lead onward. Readers get a popular Ozark romance of a mysterious shepherd, a mountain girl, and old secrets.
4768-let-s-collect-rocks-and-shells:
Let's Collect Rocks and Shells is a short booklet for beginners, published with Shell Oil Company's interest in its subjects. Its contents cover collecting seashells, what seashells are, the shell as an architect, meeting some shells, where to look, and starting a collection, with how to begin. Collecting rocks follows, with rocks made of minerals, main kinds of rocks, and collecting gems for the lucky few.

The introduction says millions of people have found pleasure, adventure, and education in collecting rocks or shells. This booklet will not tell everything, since that would need many large volumes. It aims to arouse curiosity about two delightful pastimes, broad enough to lead to a career or a satisfying hobby. Shell's name, it notes, comes from seashells brought from the Orient for mother-of-pearl buttons and knife handles, long before oil drilling. Readers get a friendly starter guide, clear and encouraging.
4914-the-motor-girls:
Margaret Penrose's Motor Girls opens with Cora Kimball and her brother Jack sparring over a mysterious object, setting the tone for a lively girls' adventure story. Cora, quick with sarcasm and ready for a joke about kindling wood, leads a circle of friends whose motoring trips bring scrapes, rivalries, and small mysteries.

The book belongs to the early automobile age, when a car meant freedom for young women as well as trouble on rough roads. Penrose keeps the dialogue brisk and the friendships warm. Readers get a light, cheerful serial adventure, written for girls who wanted heroines behind the wheel rather than waiting at home.
4930-paste-jewels:
John Kendrick Bangs's Paste Jewels gathers stories about domestic servants, all based, the author insists, on incidents he observed over ten years. With one stated exception, every servant in the tales was hired only after presenting references from responsible persons, references that could properly have gone only to domestics of sterling character.

The moral points itself: fine references proved no guard against trouble, and paste jewels glitter beside real ones in these tales of theft, deception, and household chaos. Bangs tells the stories with dry humor. Readers get a witty, slightly worldly set of servant tales, where respectability itself becomes the joke.
5145-the-heart-of-the-hills:
John Fox Jr.'s mountain novel opens in June 1912 with twin spirals of blue smoke rising over the Kentucky hills, and it stays close to that country throughout. Mountain families, feuds, and the slow arrival of the outside world shape the lives of its people, as the hills themselves, in their moods and seasons, press upon every choice.

Fox dedicated the book to his father's memory, and its affection for mountain life runs through the story. Readers will find feuds, love, and loyalty set against a landscape Fox knew well, in a novel that helped fix the popular image of Appalachia for a generation of readers.
5253-the-maid-of-the-whispering-hills:
Vingie E. Roe's Maid of the Whispering Hills, published in January 1912, is a romance of the Canadian North-West. Its chapters follow venturers, new homes, a stranger from civilisation, Nor'westers, spring trade, forest news. Gold fire follows, as a young woman's life intertwines with traders, trappers, and the peoples of the hills.

Roe dedicated the book to her mother, her father, and her little brother, long asleep on the hill at Carney. The novel offers readers a vivid frontier romance, with long trails, fellow captives. A compelling power draws its heroine onward through the whispering hills.
5268-courts-and-criminals:
Arthur Train's Courts and Criminals gathers essays written between 1905 and 1910 on the American criminal courts. Opening with the fiction that every accused man is presumed innocent, Train follows the case of a young man named Duffy, dragged to headquarters. He was photographed without leave. Train then examines how cases are prepared, how juries are swayed, and why men kill.

Train, a New York prosecutor turned writer, uses statistics on murder and conviction alongside courtroom stories. The book offers a lively, critical portrait of early twentieth-century justice. It remains readable for anyone curious about how courts really worked behind their formal rules.
5274-the-chaplet-of-pearls:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Chaplet of Pearls is a historical novel of France in the Wars of Religion. It opens with the bridal of the white and black, follows a separation and a family council. It moves through a convent bird, a wedding with crimson favours, and a king's tragedy. A palace of slaughter follows, toward the hearths and thickets of the Bocage.

Yonge sets Catholic and Huguenot loyalties against family honour and love, in the manner of her historical romances. The novel offers readers a dramatic, richly detailed picture of sixteenth-century France, where a chaplet of pearls passes through danger, disguise, and devotion.
5311-parnassus-on-wheels:
Christopher Morley's Parnassus on Wheels presents itself as the story of a woman who told it to Morley with inimitable vivacity. Morley sends the book to David Grayson of Hempfield with an acknowledgment, noting that Mrs Mifflin, unskilled in authorship, hardly realised how much her story owed to Grayson's own writings.

The tale follows a travelling book wagon, Parnassus, and the woman who buys it and takes to the road selling books. Readers get a charming, bookish road novel, celebrating reading, independence, and the open road. The story launched Morley's beloved bookseller Roger Mifflin.
5438-glenloch-girls:
Grace M. Remick wrote Glenloch Girls as the story of a pleasant winter in the lives of some everyday girls and boys. The introduction admits the tale may not sound exciting, then argues that most young people live simple lives, and that ordinary friendship can still make a good story. Ruth Shirley, one of the girls, expects changes that will test her circle.

Chapters follow three chums, a newcomer, a new club, the Social Six, caps and aprons, Christmas presents, and a lost-and-found adventure. Illustrated by Ada C. Williamson, the book favors warmth over danger. Young readers get a gentle school story about friends, clubs, and small troubles handled with kindness.
5682-fundamental-principles-of-the-metap:
Immanuel Kant's 1785 work on the foundations of morals, translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, asks what makes an act right before asking what results it brings. Kant begins from the old Greek division of knowledge into physics, ethics, and logic, then separates what we learn from experience from what reason alone can supply. Morals, he argues, need principles that hold for every rational being, not rules fitted to one person's wishes.

The book builds its case step by step. It moves from ordinary ideas of duty and good will toward a strict test for maxims. Act only on a rule you could will as a law for all. Readers need not agree with every step to gain from it, since Kant's clarity forces a reader to state plainly why an act is justified. It remains a central text for ethics, law, and any debate about duty versus outcome.
5725-english-literature-for-boys-and-gir:
H E Marshall introduces English literature to young readers in a long, story-driven survey, from the listening time of oral tale to modern writers. Early chapters cover the cattle raid of Cooley, Fingal, old Welsh storytellers, Arthur in English, Beowulf, Caedmon, Alfred the Great, Havelok the Dane, and Piers the Ploughman. Later chapters reach Chaucer at the Tabard Inn, Barbour's Bruce, and the poet kings of Scotland.

Marshall tells literary history as a chain of stories, so a child meets each writer through a tale rather than a date. Readers gain a map of English letters that is easy to follow and pleasant to read aloud. The book remains a useful family introduction, especially for homeschooling or bedtime reading, since it treats old books as adventures waiting to be heard.
5804-the-story-of-a-lamb-on-wheels:
The Story of a Lamb on Wheels follows a toy lamb through small adventures told in short chapters. The lamb wishes, meets a jolly sailor, finds a home on shore, and slides downhill into great danger. Later chapters send the lamb down a coal hole, carried away, sailing down a brook, and riding on a load of wood, until Mirabell is happy at last.

Young readers join a world where toys wake, wander, and worry, much like children themselves. The story favors gentle mishaps over real fright, with each chapter ending safely enough for bedtime. It suits early readers and read-aloud families who enjoy old-fashioned toy tales, where a lamb on wheels learns the world one bump at a time.
5830-a-garland-for-girls:
Louisa May Alcott gathers flower-named stories for girls in A Garland for Girls, affectionately inscribed to a friend. Contents include May Flowers, An Ivy Spray and Ladies' Slippers, Pansies, Water-Lilies, Poppies and Wheat, Little Button-Rose, and Mountain-Laurel and Maiden-Hair. Each story takes a flower as its emblem, weaving blossom, season, and girlhood into a gentle tale.

Readers get Alcott's warm moral storytelling at its most charming, with heroines learning kindness, patience, and courage through everyday trials. The stories favor home, friendship, and nature over grand adventure, and they suit read-aloud families and young readers. Fans of Alcott will recognize her voice here, softer than in her novels but just as sure about what matters.
6085-the-code-of-honor-or-rules-for-the-:
John Lyde Wilson, former governor of South Carolina, published his Code of Honor in 1838 as a 22-page booklet, sized to fit in the case with one's duelling pistols. An appendix of the 1777 Irish code, added before his death, reached print only in 1858, making a 46-page small book.

The code is far less bloodthirsty than many suppose, Wilson's transcribers note, but built on a closed caste and standards alien to today. A rencontre, a fight in heat of offense, counted as manslaughter, while a duel in cold blood counted as murder. Posting an offender meant publishing notice of his behavior in a club.
6111-over-prairie-trails:
Frederick Philip Grove writes Over Prairie Trails from years teaching in a small prairie town. His wife and little daughter lived near the northern timber, not far from a great lake's western shore. His wife, to round off a far-from-imperial income, took charge of a rural school with a residence.

Grove procured a buggy and horse and drove home Fridays after school, returning Sunday evenings. The trip ran sixty-eight miles each way in clement seasons, and ninety from the second week of January when straight roads failed. Chapters on farms, fog, dawn and diamonds, snow, wind and waves, and skies and scares follow the trail.
6128-his-sombre-rivals:
E. P. Roe writes His Sombre Rivals with regret akin to sadness, taking leave of people who became very real to him, whose joys and sorrows he made his own. Though a Northern man, he believes Southern readers will feel he sought justice for their motives.

At distance from the Civil War, Roe argues, passion and prejudice should sink below the horizon, as among surviving soldiers arrayed against each other they have practically disappeared. Stern conflict taught mutual respect, convincing Northern men they fought Americans whose patriotism was as pure as their own. The novel pleads for large-minded reunion.
6360-half-a-dozen-girls:
Anna Chapin Ray offers memories of a happy, naughty childhood, dedicated to her parents, with Kingsley's verse on being good and doing noble things. Polly Adams chants a rhyme at a guest, little girl with a curl, very good when good and horrid when bad. Then she climbs down from the front gate, shakes her curly head, and runs indoors. Upstairs her mother and aunt sew behind closed blinds on a sultry July day, to locust whir and a rocking chair's creak.

The Adams family opens a book of six girls, their mothers, maids, and mischief. Molly asks why a cross maid is kept, and Polly answers that nothing else can be got. Ray writes childhood as it feels, warm, funny, and unforced, where a rhyme, a gate, and a hot afternoon hold a world. The book is a girl's story of home, not of adventure far away.
6432-betty-wales-sophomore-a-story-for-g:
Margaret Warde, author of Betty Wales, Freshman, Junior, Senior, and B.A., follows Betty into sophomore year in 1905. Betty sits on the one bare spot of her Belden House room floor, sighing with relief and weariness. She tells a green lizard on pillows that things are out of trunks, if not yet in their places. At quarter to eight, Eleanor Watson raps, and Betty leaps over cups and saucers, knocks a Japanese screen onto a bed, and hugs her friend.

Isn't it great to be back, Betty asks, setting the screen up and moving trays so they can sit on the bed. Later, Betty advises Roberta, who gets on with children and older people but not her age, to practise as she would chemistry problems. Figure out what freshmen like, give it to them, and have a party with the Jabberwock. Warde writes college girls' life with humour and warmth.
6804-general-history-for-colleges-and-hi:
P. V. N. Myers bases his General History for colleges and high schools on his earlier Ancient History and his Medieval and Modern History. In places he shifts perspective and proportion, yet the book follows the same lines as those earlier works. A frontispiece shows the Attic plains with a glimpse of the Acropolis at Athens.

Myers admits that, in so wide a field, some error is bound to slip in, though he took great care to check facts and to give the latest finds and criticism. The result is a broad, schoolroom survey from ancient times to modern days. General History is a solid, old-style textbook, clear and well ordered for students.
6850-esther-a-book-for-girls:
Rosa Nouchette Carey tells Esther's story from her last day at Redmayne House to her arrival at Combe Manor, with Dot, Uncle Geoffrey, and an old house at Milnthorpe ahead. A flitting, neighbors over the way, Flurry and Flossy, and the Cedars follow, with a wish for a Dot of her own and a nurse named Miss Ruth. Esther feels she is not like other girls.

A smugglers' cave, a long night, a brave girl's praise, and a letter from home lead toward Christmas and a walk to Eltham Green. Carey writes with gentle, domestic warmth. Esther is a kind, old-style girls' book of home, friendship, and growing up.
7144-while-the-billy-boils:
Henry Lawson's While the Billy Boils gathers bush stories in two series, opening with an old mate of your father's, settling on the land, and Enter Mitchell. Stiffner and Jim, thirdly Bill, when the sun went down, and the man who forgot Hungerford follow, with a camp fire yarn, his country after all, and a day on a selection. That there dog of mine going blind, Arvie Aspinall's alarm clock, and stragglers lead to the union burying its dead.

On the Edge of a Plain, In a Dry Season, He's Come Back, Another of Mitchell's Plans, Steelman, Drifted Back, and Mitchell Doesn't Believe in the Sack follow. Shooting the moon, his father's mate, and an echo from the old bark school close the first series, while the second brings the drover's wife, Steelman's pupil, and an unfinished love story. Lawson writes the bush in yarns of mateship and hard times.
7430-familiar-spanish-travels:
W. D. Howells first met Spain as a boy of seventeen, reading Spanish tales of the vanished Moorish kingdom in a little room under the stairs. Familiar Spanish Travels, published in 1913, returns to that boyhood dream as an old traveler. The route runs through San Sebastian and Biscay, Burgos in its bitter cold, Valladolid, and Madrid, then on to Toledo, Cordova, Seville, Granada, and Ronda.

Howells writes familiarly, as the title says: not as a guidebook author ticking sights, but as a friend telling what he saw and felt. He lingers over markets, cathedrals, and the contrast between Moorish past and Spanish present. For readers who know his Italian travels, this is the Spanish companion, warm, observant, and unhurried.
7546-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
William Dean Howells, the dean of American realism, wrote novels, criticism, and essays for half a century, and this volume gathers quotations from his writings with images. The entries show his mind at work: absolutely, so positively, so almost aggressively truthful. An account of one's reading is an account of one's life. Affections will not be bidden.

Other sayings touch his age's nerves: industrial slavery, lewd literature giving sanction to lewdness in life, and critics who are in no sense the legislators of literature. Clemens, he wrote, was sole and incomparable, the Lincoln of American literature, and Dickens rescued Christmas from gloom. The collection is a portrait of Howells himself: honest, humane, and quietly radical about truth in fiction.
771-biographical-notes-on-the-pseudonymo:
Charlotte Brontë wrote these short pieces to clear up a common error: that the works signed Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell came from one hand. She states plainly that three sisters wrote them, Currer being herself, Ellis being Emily, and Acton being Anne. The notice was prefixed to a reprint of Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey.

Brontë tells how the sisters chose male pen names, how their books were received, and how Emily and Anne lived and died. Her tone is proud and mournful, defending her sisters' fame while mourning their loss. The pieces are essential reading for anyone who wants the true story behind the Bell name, told by the sister who survived.
7867-crooked-trails:
Frederic Remington's Crooked Trails, first published in 1898 and pictured by the author, opens in a San Antonio club. The Deacon promises a talk with Colonel Rip Ford of the old Texas Rangers. White-haired and bent yet unwithered, Ford sinks into an armchair to tell tales.

Contents run from how law got into the chaparral and the blue quail of the cactus through a sergeant of the orphan troop. Massai's crooked trail, cracker cowboys of Florida, and the Soledad girls follow. Through Rangers, cowboys, and frontier fights, Remington records a West already fading.
8502-common-diseases-of-farm-animals:
R. A. Craig, a doctor of veterinary medicine, wrote Common Diseases of Farm Animals for farmers and stockmen. The frontispiece warns, with a picture of an insanitary dairy stable and yards, that disease and financial loss are to be expected when animals are kept in filth. Contents open with a general discussion of disease, and diagnosis and symptoms, before treating diseases in turn.

Craig's manual belongs to the age when veterinary science reached the farm, and clean stables became an economic argument. Readers get practical advice on recognizing and treating illness in cattle, horses, sheep, and pigs. The book interests historians of agriculture, and anyone curious about animal care before modern drugs.
8590-auld-licht-idyls:
J. M. Barrie, later famous for Peter Pan, sketches the strict Auld Licht folk of Thrums, his fictional version of his native Kirriemuir in Scotland. A schoolmaster narrator opens the book in his glen school-house, wakened by a starving sparrow at a frosted window. The chapters move through the kirk, the school, courtships, funerals, and a small literary club. Lads and lasses, old dominies, and village worthies fill the pages.

Barrie's humour is gentle but not soft: the Auld Lichts' stern religion, thrift, and pride are shown with affection and with a clear eye for their narrowness. The idylls made his name, proving a Scots village could carry a whole book of stories. Readers who know Barrie only from Neverland will find here the roots of his art, in dialect, memory, and the comedy of small-town dignity.
8939-with-edged-tools:
Henry Seton Merriman wrote this adventure novel of trade and peril in Africa, first in the late 1800s. Its hero, an Englishman of two generations of traders, sails to the West African coast to seek ivory and a lost secret, facing rivals, fever, and war among the trading stations. The title points to tools that cut both ways.

Chapters move from London farewells to Loango, to deals struck in bad faith, panics, and a race to the rescue. Merriman keeps the pace brisk and the moral lines clear, though modern readers will note its age in its view of Africa. It still works as a swift, old-style tale of risk and nerve.
9048-ballads-founded-on-anecdotes-relati:
William Hayley wrote these ballads in 1805, with prints designed and cut by William Blake, for young readers. Each poem grows from a true tale about an animal: a loyal dog, a kind horse, or some other beast that showed courage or love. Hayley states his aim at once, that the book is meant for boys and girls.

The verse is simple and moral, praising faith, kindness, and care for creatures that cannot speak for themselves. Blake's art gives the small book extra worth, since his prints are now prized far past Hayley's verse. Together they make a charming relic of a time when children's books taught through story and song.
9923-the-box-with-broken-seals:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's 1919 thriller opens in a Chicago hotel, where the Englishman James Crawshay and his American fellow traveler Hobson wait, uneasy, for the chief of police. Both men have just finished a long journey, and something crooked about their business waits to be explained.

The broken seals of the title point to a secret opened before its time, and the story follows Crawshay through suspicion, pursuit, and revelation in Oppenheim's brisk popular manner. Readers who like Edwardian crime tales with an American setting will enjoy its quick pace and confident hero.
a-book-of-remarkable-criminals:
H. B. Irving wrote these true-crime lives of notorious offenders. The contents promise studies of Charles Peace, the burglar and murderer; Robert Butler of the Dunedin murders; the poisoners Derues and Dr. Castaing; Professor Webster; the mysterious Mr. Holmes; and a closing part on partnerships in crime, from the Widow Gras to the Fenayrou case and Eyraud and Bompard.

Irving's introduction argues that crime deserves serious study: the connection between motive and act, he writes, is as necessary to the jurist as to the student of human nature. Each life is then told as a narrative, from early years through trial and execution or decline. Irving, a lawyer's son steeped in famous trials, writes as an essayist rather than a sensation-monger, which gives the book its lasting place in crime writing.
a-book-of-scoundrels:
Charles Whibley profiles famous rogues of past centuries with open delight in their skill. His contents list Captain Hind, Moll Cutpurse, Jonathan Wild, Ralph Briscoe, and Gilderoy, then Jack Sheppard, Cartouche, George Barrington, Deacon Brodie, and Charles Peace. Each life is told from the records and old pamphlets.

Whibley pairs many of his rogues and draws parallels between them, thief against thief. He treats a masterly theft as a kind of dark art and writes with wit rather than moral horror. The chapters mix true history, anecdote, and shrewd character study. Readers who enjoy old London crime and highway romance will find a rich store here.
a-century-of-roundels:
Algernon Charles Swinburne fills a whole book with one small form: the roundel, a short poem with a refrain that returns like a bell note. This second edition of 1883, from Chatto and Windus, dedicates the volume to Christina G. Rossetti. The contents number the poems to a hundred, as the title promises.

In Harbour, The Way of the Wind, Had I Wist, Time and Life, and A Baby's Death stand among the early titles. A roundel on the death of Richard Wagner joins them. Two preludes are named for Lohengrin and Tristan. Swinburne makes the tight form sing of children, seasons, friendship, and grief. The book is a jewel box of Victorian lyric craft.
a-garland-for-girls:
A Garland for Girls, by Louisa May Alcott, gathers seven stories named for flowers, written, she says, for her own amusement during enforced seclusion. Alcott signed the preface in September 1887 and inscribed the book to R A Lawrence, her grateful friend. The flowers that were her solace in illness suggested the titles: May Flowers, Pansies, Water-Lilies, Poppies and Wheat, Little Button-Rose, and two more sprays of blossom.

The first tale opens in Boston, where six girls, descendants of Pilgrim Fathers as Alcott notes, form a club for mental improvement and call it the Mayflower Club. Each story in the garland ties a girl's work, pride, or kindness to its flower. Alcott writes for the readers who grew up with her: young women earning, helping, and deciding, with sentiment kept on a short stem and moralizing woven into incident rather than preached.
an-enquiry-concerning-the-principles-of-:
David Hume's Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals recasts his earlier moral philosophy in clearer form. Hume explains in his advertisement that the work restates ideas first printed in his Treatise of Human Nature. This edition follows the posthumous printing of 1777. The subject is why people praise some traits and blame others.

Sections treat benevolence, justice, and political society in turn. Hume argues that utility, meaning usefulness to people, explains much of our approval. Other chapters sort qualities that serve ourselves and qualities that please others at once. Four appendices handle moral sentiment, self-love, justice, and disputes over words. The book remains a founding text of modern ethics, valued for its calm tone and its test of moral rules against human feeling.
b09-brant-ship-of-fools:
Sebastian Brant, a Strasbourg lawyer, launched his Narrenschiff, The Ship of Fools, in German in 1494. The poem loads every kind of fool onto one ship bound for folly's land. Alexander Barclay turned it into English verse in 1509, and that rendering, in T H Jamieson's 1874 edition, fills this text.

Across 157 chapters Brant mocks greed, vanity, bad manners, false learning, and folly in church and state. Each fool gets a portrait in verse sharp enough to sting and broad enough to fit any age. The image of the ship sailed on through European art and letters, from Bosch to Bruegel. The satire still lands.
betty-wales-sophomore-a-story-for-girls:
Betty Wales, Sophomore, a story for girls, is credited on its title page to Margaret Warde. Warde's contents open with Moving In and Eleanor's Freshman. Parades and Parties, Points of View, and On Ambition carry the college year. The First Four, In the Argus Sanctum, and A Problem in Ethics raise the stakes toward midyears. Eva Nagel illustrated the 1905 volume.

Betty's sophomore year is the middle of a five book progress through college and beyond it. Freshman, junior, senior, and B A volumes stand around this one. The author's name on the title page is a pen name, and the series became a standard of girls' college fiction. Classes, the college paper, and friendship's ethics fill its world. No one fails out of Warde's college. The examinations that matter are social and moral, and Betty Wales passes them in a way meant to be copied.
biographical-notes-on-the-pseudonymous-b:
Charlotte Bronte wrote this biographical notice to end a mistake: readers believed Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell were one person. She states plainly that the Bells were three sisters, and that Ellis and Acton, Emily and Anne, were now dead. The notice prefaced a reprint of Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey.

Charlotte describes Emily's fierce, home-loving nature and Anne's quieter patience, borne through illness by firm Christian faith. She watched them, she writes, follow the same path at different steps toward early graves. A companion piece, her editor's preface, defends Emily's rough genius. Together these short pieces are essential documents for understanding the Bronte sisters and their chosen masks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acquaviva-car:
Acquaviva is the name of several Italian cardinals, and this entry sketches seven of them. Francesco, born at Naples in 1665 of the Dukes of Atri, served under four popes, was made cardinal and Bishop of Sabina by Clement XI, and died in 1723. Giovanni Vincenzo, Bishop of Melfi and Rapolla, became cardinal-priest in 1542 and died in 1566. Giulio, nuncio of Pius V to Philip II of Spain, was made cardinal by that pope and attended him on his deathbed.

Ottavio the elder, Archbishop of Naples in 1605, helped convert Henri IV. Ottavio the younger, made cardinal in 1654, served as legate in Viterbo and Romagna, curbing the banditti there. Troiano, made cardinal in 1732, represented the Spanish kings in the Curia and influenced the conclave electing Benedict XIV in 1740. Pasquale, made cardinal in 1773, closes the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-vessels:
Altar vessels centre on the chalice, holding the Eucharistic wine and water. It should be gold, or silver gilt inside, or a silver cup gilt inside with base and stem of any solid, clean, becoming metal. Stannum, a tin-lead alloy, is also allowed with a gilt interior. The paten, holding the altar bread, matches the chalice's material, gilt on its concave side if not gold, its edge thin and sharp to gather particles from the corporal.

The ciborium keeps consecrated particles for the laity's Communion, of any solid decent material, even gilt copper. The ostensorium, a glass-framed shrine of gold, silver, brass, or gilt copper, exposes the Blessed Sacrament publicly. A chalice loses consecration when unfit for use, as when the slightest break appears near the cup's bottom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angels:
Angel, from Latin angelus and Greek aggelos, from Hebrew for one going or one sent, means messenger. The Hebrew word means a divine or human messenger, rendered aggelos by the Septuagint, with both meanings. The Latin version distinguishes the spirit-messenger from humans, using angelus for the one and legatus or nuntius for the other. In a few passages the Latin version misleads, using angelus where nuntius would fit better, as in Isaiah 18:2.

Only the spirit-messenger concerns this article. It discusses the term's meaning, the angels' offices and names, good and evil spirits, the choirs, and appearances. Districts are allotted to angels termed their princes, as in the Apocalyptic angels of the seven churches. De Coelesti Hierarchia, ascribed to Saint Denis the Areopagite, treats of the hierarchies and orders of angels, though it dates centuries later. Its doctrine of the choirs has been received with extraordinary unanimity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-sch:
Apostolic schools are schools that train boys for the foreign missions, where the church is not yet normally organized. In settled lands, junior seminaries begin the training of diocesan clergy and theological seminaries complete it. Mission lands, by contrast, depend on foreign mission colleges and on apostolic schools to supply priests. Their object is to foster vocations, or calls to mission work, among youths who might otherwise never reach a seminary.

As distinct from junior seminaries, apostolic schools trace their origin to Father Alberic de Foresta, a Jesuit who lived from 1818 to 1876. He found many fine societies for prayer and mission funds, yet judged them weak without a supply of men to preach and give the sacraments. Experience in guiding souls convinced him that pious youths, held back by poverty or other bars, could still become missionaries if a school took them in hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-appeals:
Appeals gives a comprehensive view of the church's positive law on appeals within the church court system. It leaves the nature of that court and the pope's right to receive appeals to other articles. An appeal is defined as a legal application to a superior authority for redress against an injury from a lower authority's act. The lower authority is called the judge from whom appeal is made, the higher the appellate judge or court. Appeals divide into judicial and extrajudicial kinds.

A judicial appeal attacks acts of the lower authority in its official role as judge at any stage of proceedings. It covers not only a final sentence but also an interlocutory sentence, one given during the case. The long article then works through kinds, effects, time limits, and procedure, giving canon lawyers and historians the full framework by which church judgments could be challenged and corrected.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bath-and-well:
Bath and Wells is an ancient diocese coextensive with Somerset, England, though its first bishop under that exact title came only in 1244. Æthelhelm, later Archbishop of Canterbury, first ruled there from 909 to 914, choosing Wells's secular church as cathedral. Rivalry followed between Wells's secular canons and the monks of Glastonbury and Bath, with Wells struggling.

Bishop Gisa (1060-88) found Wells small and poor, its canons begging bread, and rebuilt it with lands from Edward, Harold, and William the Conqueror. His successor John de Villula undid much by moving the see to Bath in 1088, using its abbey as cathedral. Robert of Lewes (1136-66) rebuilt Wells's cathedral and arranged a settlement, and the diocese held three archdeaconries: Bath, Wells, and Taunton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bells:
Bells get a wide-ranging survey in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, treated in five parts that move from origins to law. The entry opens with ancient and early Christian uses of bells and sounding instruments, then turns to the rite of blessing them. That blessing, with its prayers and anointing, gives a bell its place in church life.

Later sections cover daily uses, from calling worshippers to marking deaths and alarms, and then inscriptions and old examples that survive. A closing part sets out points of canon law on who may bless, ring, and remove bells. The entry joins liturgy, craft, and church rule in one reference piece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-kells:
The Book of Kells, an Irish manuscript of the Four Gospels, ranks as the choicest relic of Irish art. Also called the Book of Columba, it likely comes from Iona, and the Annals of Ulster record the theft of Columba's Gospel in 1006, probably this book. Tradition makes it Columba's own work, but its script and ornament place it no earlier than the late seventh or early eighth century.

Gerald of Wales saw it at Kildare in the twelfth century and praised it warmly. It later rested at Kells in Meath until 1541, and Archbishop Ussher gave it to Trinity College, Dublin, where it remains the library's treasure. Two unknown scribes seem to have written and painted it in black, red, purple, and yellow ink. Its spirals, trumpet patterns, beast interlacements, and ribbon plaits show Irish design at its inventive peak, though some ornaments stay unfinished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brussels:
Brussels, capital of Belgium, held 612,041 people at the end of 1905 with its eight suburban communes. It grew on the little Senne, now arched over by inner boulevards, and rose on the inland trade road between the Low Countries and Cologne. Canals link it to the Sambre and the Scheldt, and it has borne the title of seaport since 1895.

Tradition credits Saint Gery, Bishop of Cambrai, with a village and chapel on a Senne island late in the sixth century. First named Brosella, marsh dwelling, near the ninth century's end, it passed through Gerberga's dower to Lorraine's dukes. Charles of Lorraine made it his home and brought Saint Gudule's bones from Mortzelle in 979, making her the town's patron. On his son Otto's death in 1004, Lambert Balderic took Brussels, Vilvorde, and Louvain, seed of the duchy of Brabant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carolingian-s:
Carolingian schools grew from a Merovingian palace school, the scola palatina, that trained young Frankish nobles in war and court ceremony rather than letters. Literary teaching in those days belonged to monastic and cathedral schools. With Charlemagne's accession in 768, reform began in the palace school itself and spread by imperial decree to schools across his vast empire.

The palace school changed from tactics and manners to learning from 780, once victories over Lombards, Saxons, and Saracens allowed it. Real success came only with Alcuin's arrival at Aachen in 782. Alcuin headed the emperor's palace school and joined his council on all educational matters, becoming Charlemagne's prime minister of education and bringing York's learning tradition. Monastic, episcopal, and village schools carried the revival forward, despite war and pillage, to the dawn of university teaching in the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-summ:
A Catholic summer school gathers clergy and laity in the summer months for lectures and special courses, fostering intellectual culture in harmony with Christian faith along university-extension lines. The movement began with the Champlain Summer School. It was founded at New London, Connecticut, in 1892. In 1893 it settled permanently at Cliff Haven, New York.

Other schools followed. The Columbian Summer School opened at Madison, Wisconsin, in 1895, later moving to Milwaukee. A winter school began at New Orleans in 1896, and the Maryland Summer School in 1900. The article traces the roots of the movement in reading circles, university extension, and summer institutes, including Isaac Hecker's library work and the young men's lyceums.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-mathi:
An entry on Charles Mathieu Schols, a Dutch civil engineer and geodesist, a measurer of the earth's surface, born at Maastricht in 1849. He trained at the Delft polytechnic, taught at the Royal Military Academy at Breda, and published a textbook on surveying in 1879. Offered the Delft chair of geodesy and surveying in 1878, he was elected to the Royal Academy of Sciences in 1880 and published a stream of papers on the mathematics of mapping.

Schols wrote on computing distance and direction from latitude and longitude, on joining small survey triangles to larger nets, and on map projections, the ways of flattening the curved earth onto paper. He also worked on error theory, pure mathematics, and bridge stresses, and he helped write a textbook on hydraulic architecture, the building of waterworks. He prepared and supervised the new national survey of Holland begun in 1886. He died at Delft in 1897.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
The Clerks Regular of the Pious Schools, also called Piarists and Scolopi, are a religious order founded at Rome in 1597 by Saint Joseph Calasanctius. A Confraternity of Christian Doctrine member, he taught country people and saw the need for early religious instruction of poor children. Antonio Brendoni, Santa Dorotea in Trastevere's pastor, gave him two rooms, soon joined by two other priests.

As attendance grew, Calasanctius moved the school into the city and lived there with companions. A later move to the Vestri Palace began community life, and Clement the Eighth approved the work with a yearly allowance for rent. Inspection by Cardinals Antoniani and Baronius satisfied critics, and Paul the Fifth approved still more warmly. On 25 March 1617 Calasanctius and his companions took the religious habit. Gregory the Fifteenth made the congregation a religious order on 18 November 1621.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cruelty-to-an:
A moral entry surveys attitudes to cruelty toward animals from pagan antiquity to Catholic doctrine. Pythagoras and Empedocles first urged kindness, holding that human souls pass into animal bodies after death, so animals share human rights. Cicero condemned that error, while Roman law still protected useful beasts.

The Old Testament forbade muzzling the treading ox and yoking ox and ass together. The New Testament is nearly silent, and the Fathers say little. Scholastics, above all St. Thomas, condemned needless suffering chiefly for its harm to the doer's character. Catholic doctrine, the entry argues, grants animals no rights yet denounces cruelty vigorously. Excessive fondness, it warns, is no sure index of moral worth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cure-of-souls:
A canon law entry defines the cure of souls, in Latin cura animarum, as a clerical office with a set district. Its holder teaches the faithful by sermons and warnings, and makes them holy through the sacraments, by lawful appointment. The pope holds it for the whole Church, bishops in their dioceses, and parish priests in their parishes.

Others share it under these leaders. Missionaries in lands without sees share the pope's care for those regions, and parish curates serve parts of a parish under their pastor. Its object is the salvation of souls, carrying on Christ's mission on earth. A priest's mission comes from the Church alone. It flows through apostolic succession in two forms: holy orders, passed on by bishops, and jurisdiction, passed on by the living teaching office headed by the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devotional-me:
A survey of devotional medals, pieces of metal struck or cast like coins but never used as money, bearing an image, device, or inscription for memory's sake. Religious medals outdo secular ones in variety. They mark persons, shrines, and events, first Communions and ordinations, and mysteries of faith. They teach piety, badge associations, protect the wearer, and carry indulgences.

Early Christian examples were long doubted. De Rossi's 1869 article settled some as genuine. The Middle Ages left little trace, and the Renaissance brought medals proper into popular post-Reformation use. Classes follow. Plague medals show Sebastian, Roch, and shrine views. Other medals mark Eucharistic miracles such as Seefeld, and private medals mark baptisms and weddings. Legend medals close the list, led by the cross said to have reached Saint Ulrich before battle in 955.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-christi:
Angels were seldom shown in Christian art before Constantine. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names the oldest angel fresco, an Annunciation of the second century in the cemetery of Saint Priscilla. In the cemetery of Saints Peter and Marcellinus, Wilpert found a third-century Annunciation, where Gabriel likewise appears as a human figure, robed in tunic and pallium. The Good Angel of a fourth-century fresco of the judgment of Vibia also wears human dress, as a sacred personage.

The winged angel, though Scripture offers ample warrant, does not appear before Constantine, likely because wings would recall favorite subjects of classical art. The entry then traces angels in litanies and churches, with Michael and Gabriel invoked just after the Trinity. Umbria was famed for angel churches, and the East raised many to Saint Michael.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical annals belong to the historical writing of the Middle Ages, classed with chronicles and lives of saints. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that chronicles began in Greece, while annals first appear among Romans. In the Middle Ages chronicle covered every form of history, though at first it meant only a chronological table. Pagan history no longer appealed to Christian writers, who sought a history centered on the kingdom of God.

To the new generation the heart of history lay in the misfortunes of the Jewish nation, a theme Roman historians ignored. Christians needed a general history in tune with their ideal. The entry follows the annal form from its Roman roots through Carolingian writers such as Einhard, with Kurze and Waitz among its guides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-episcopal-san:
Episcopal sandals are low shoes, more like slippers, worn with liturgical stockings at pontifical solemn Mass. Unlike ancient sandals, mere soles tied by straps, they have a leather sole and an upper of silk or velvet, often embroidered. No cross is required on them, since at Rome that mark is a papal privilege alone. The stockings, called caligae, are silk, knitted or sewn.

Only bishops may wear sandals and caligae by right; abbots and other prelates need a special papal privilege. They are used only at pontifical Mass and ordinations, never at Confirmations or solemn Vespers. Their colour follows the day, but there are no black sandals or stockings, since they are not used at Masses for the dead or on Good Friday. They belong to the Latin rite alone and are unknown in Eastern rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernst-of-hess:
Ernst of Hesse-Rheinfels, a landgrave, was born on 9 December 1623 at Cassel and died on 12 May 1693 at Cologne. Moritz, Landgrave of Hesse-Cassel, was his father, and Ernst was his sixth son. Ernst and his brother Hermann founded the collateral lines of Hesse-Rheinfels and Hesse-Rotenburg after Moritz resigned the government in 1627 to his son Wilhelm V. His conversion to the Catholic Faith stirred controversial literature, and that is why he figures prominently in his country's religious history.

His mother raised him under strict discipline, and his instruction in the Reformed Church received the utmost attention. In 1642 he joined the Hessian army, where he proved an able commander of troops fighting on Sweden's side in the Thirty Years' War. While visiting the Hessian General Geyso, imprisoned at Gesecke, he was himself arrested and taken prisoner to Paderborn. Talk there with the royal army chaplain began his conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-espousals:
An espousal is a contract of future marriage between a man and a woman, who are thereby affianced. The law governing this contract was amended by the decree Ne Temere, published 2 August 1907 and effective 19 April 1908. For the old legislation see Betrothal; the present article is confined to the new. The decree enacts that only written espousals, signed by both parties and by the parish priest, the ordinary, or two witnesses, are valid and beget canonical effects.

If a party cannot write, this is noted, and another witness signs with the priest, the ordinary, or the two witnesses. Until Easter 1908 no written document was prescribed for espousals, except for Spain. Before, the promise of marriage bound the parties according to prevailing law or custom. That caused difficulties which necessitated this law. Private, clandestine espousals are henceforth of no value in the eyes of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evangelical-c:
The Evangelical Counsels, also called the Counsels of Perfection, are Gospel counsels for those who would do more than the bare minimum for heaven. Christ laid down precepts binding on all, above all the Ten Commandments, as the needful condition of eternal life. Beside them he taught counsels, not binding on all, for those aiming at Christian perfection as far as it can be reached on earth. Christ told the rich young man first to keep the commandments, then, if he would be perfect, to sell all and give to the poor.

The three chief counsels answer the three great goods of this world: riches, pleasures of the flesh, and honors. Poverty frees the soul from riches, chastity from fleshly pleasure, and obedience from self-love and rank. A soul may be saved without them, but reaches heaven more surely with them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-false-decreta:
The False Decretals are a forged set of papal letters from the ninth century. They circulated under the name of Isidore Mercator, or Pseudo-Isidore. The collection mixes genuine texts with about a hundred forged letters. Its three parts cover early popes, councils, and later decretal law.

Scholars exposed the forgery through anachronisms in dates, language, and law. Blondel's critique of 1628 proved decisive against the collection. The Ballerini brothers and Hinschius later produced critical editions of the texts. The article traces the forgery's spread and its effect on church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-fool:
The Feast of Fools was a licensed medieval revel held near New Year's Day. It grew from the subdeacons' festival on the Circumcision feast. Deacons, priests, and choristers each had their own December days. The subdeacons' day became a feast of the lower clergy and fools' guilds.

Its license echoed the pagan Saturnalia, when slaves stood equal to masters. Church authorities condemned its excesses again and again, often in vain. At Paris in 1199 the bishop curbed, but did not ban, the revel. The feast's core idea was brief reversal, with the lowly raised high.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-guar:
The Feast of Guardian Angels honours the angels assigned to each individual person. Local at first, it reached Cordova in 1579 and Toledo and Valencia soon after. Paul V placed it in the general calendar in 1608. Clement X later made it obligatory for the whole Church on 2 October.

The belief itself is ancient, though the feast is comparatively recent. Early liturgies already praised angelic protection and intercession for mortal men. The Mass texts stress the angels' threefold office of praise and guidance. In Germany the feast is kept on the first Sunday of September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-counc:
General Councils are lawfully convened assemblies of church leaders and theologians to settle doctrine and discipline by common deliberation. Council and synod mean the same, though mere worship meetings and diocesan synods fall short of the name, and unlawful gatherings earn the titles of robber synods. The entry defines the thing before it sorts its kinds.

Its heads run from classification and history through the pope's share in calling, guiding, and confirming councils, to who may sit, how many must come, and how business moves. The deepest questions close the work: whether councils err, how papal and conciliar infallibility fit, whether a council stands above the pope, and whether it can depose him. Definition, facts, and theory each get their turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-and-go:
Gospel and Gospels is a general article on the word Gospel, usually a written record of Christ's words and deeds. It likely comes from the Anglo-Saxon god, good, and spell, to tell. It matches the Greek euangelion, good tidings, and the Latin Evangelium. A Catholic Encyclopedia article sets out the other meanings of euangelion in the body of the piece.

The first four historical books of the New Testament carry titles such as Euangelion kata Matthaion, which, however ancient, do not go back to the authors themselves. The Muratorian Canon, Clement of Alexandria, and Irenaeus witness to the headings in the latter part of the second century. Their early currency suggests they were prefixed in the first part of that century, once the four narratives were collected.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grace-at-meal:
Grace at Meals is an article on prayer at table from apostolic times, when Paul counseled doing all to the glory of God. Clement of Alexandria held it fitting to praise the Creator before nourishment and to sing his praises over the things created. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the ancient formulae behind the Roman Benedicite and Graces.

Tertullian shows third-century Christians signing the cross at table, praying before reclining, and closing the feast with prayer. Archaeology has found cup-bases reading Drink in Christ and Drink piously. One ancient formula, in a fourth-century treatise wrongly ascribed to Athanasius, thanks the Father for the Resurrection. It prays the scattered Church be gathered as bread is made one. In the Roman liturgy the Benedicite and Graces use Psalms 149 and 33, with Psalm 1 at midday and Psalm 116 in the evening.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grace-before-:
Grace before Meals is an article on thanksgiving over food, where grace in pre-Elizabethan English always took the plural graces and means nothing but thanksgiving. Gratitude for bounty is not exclusively Christian, yet following the Saviour's own example the obligation was emphasized from the beginning. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces the practice from Paul and Aristides to the Breviary.

Paul gave thanks before eating in the sight of all. About 123 Aristides declared Christians render God thanks over food and drink. Tertullian wrote that prayer is tasted before the banquet and ends the feast, and Prudentius composed hymns Before Food and After Food. In religious orders the custom was much insisted on, with a section in Chapter 43 of Benedict's Rule, and schools and colleges kept their own metrical forms, some surviving today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-great-falls:
Great Falls is a diocese created by Pius X on 18 May 1904, covering eleven counties in eastern Montana over 94,158 square miles. Its titular city takes its name from the Missouri's falls, 533 feet in cascades yielding 340,000 horsepower, ranking next to Niagara in beauty and mechanical value. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a mission land turned manufacturing centre.

Father De Smet and companions first celebrated Mass in the territory at Fort Benton in 1850. Jesuits founded Indian missions as early as 1841. At Saint Peter's Mission, now the Ursuline mother-house of Montana, 2732 baptisms of Indians were recorded from 1855 to 1879. Cheap power feeds flour, plaster, and iron works and a smelter turning out over one hundred million pounds of copper a year, and the city ranks next to Butte in population.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guardian-ange:
Catholic teaching on guardian angels holds that each soul has an angel charged with guarding it from birth. Yet the entry stresses that this has never been defined as an article of faith. It is, in St. Jerome's phrase, the mind of the Church. The belief itself runs through pagan antiquity, Babylonian monuments, and the writings of Menander, Plutarch, and Plotinus.

Scripture carries the doctrine from Old Testament guides and protectors, in Genesis, Exodus, Tobias, and Daniel, to the New Testament's sharper statements in Matthew and Hebrews. St. Thomas holds that only the lowest angelic orders serve as guardians, acting on senses and imagination but not on the will, while Scotus and Durandus allow any angel that rank. The guardians stay with us even after death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-nails:
The Holy Nails raise a long-debated question: was Christ crucified with three nails or four? Early medieval art strongly supports four nails, and some historical writers favour that view, though none earlier than Gregory of Tours. In the thirteenth century, western art began to show the feet placed one over the other and pierced by a single nail.

That three-nail view matches Nonnus, Socrates, and a poem attributed to Gregory Nazianzen. More recent criticism notes that the two earliest Crucifixion images show no nails in the feet at all. Ambrose and other early writers imply only two nails, and Ambrose says Helena had one nail made into a bridle for Constantine. The entry sifts art, texts, and relic claims with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-oils:
Holy oils, or olea sacra, are blessed oils whose symbolic meaning matches their natural uses. They sweeten, strengthen, and make supple, and the church uses them so in its rites. Liturgical blessing of oil is very ancient. Serapion's fourth-century Prayer Book and the Apostolic Constitutions show it, as does a Syriac document from the fifth or sixth century.

Serapion's book gives a formula for blessing oil and chrism for the newly baptized, when baptism and confirmation formed one ceremony. It gives separate blessings for oil of the sick, water, and bread. The prayer asks Christ to grant his creatures power for curing the sick, purifying souls, driving away impure spirits, and wiping out sins. Old Testament oil consecrated priests, kings, and altars, and served in sacrifices and purifications.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospitals:
Hospitals began as places where strangers or visitors were received, from the Latin hospes, a guest. Only over time did the word narrow to institutions for the care of the sick. That change tracks a long development under religious, political, economic, social, and scientific influences. The modern hospital, in this view, joins natural human care for suffering with Christian charity and medical skill.

Pagan antiquity already shows humane practice among civilized peoples, though some tribes killed the feeble. Princess Macha founded an early Irish hospital in 300 BC, and the Buddhist king Asoka set up hospitals for men and animals in 252 BC. The entry follows hospitals from those beginnings through Christian foundations, medieval houses, and modern scientific institutions across the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infidels:
Those who have not been baptized are the people this entry calls infidels, from a Latin root meaning lack of faith. The name covers pagans who do not know the true God, and also Jews and Muslims, who worship God yet do not recognize Jesus Christ. Catechumens, still preparing for baptism, fall under the term in strict use, though early ages often called them Christians instead.

Baptized Christians outside the Catholic Church are not infidels in this language but non-Catholics. Baptism already makes a person a subject and child of the Church, even a rebellious one. The entry then maps how each group stands toward the Church and her laws. That distinction shaped mission policy, marriage rules, and the Church's claim over baptized persons everywhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-hessels:
Jean Hessels, a Louvain theologian born in 1522 and dead in 1566, taught eight years at Parc before taking the university theology chair. Like his senior colleague Baius, he drew theology from the Fathers, above all Augustine, rather than the Schoolmen, yet never strayed from received doctrine.

In 1559 Hessels went with Jansen and Baius to Trent, helped draft the decree on invoking saints, relics, and images, and faced Scholastic critics for leaving beaten paths. Back home he turned his energy against Protestants, defended the Immaculate Conception against Baius himself. He argued for papal infallibility in a work appended to his 1565 refutation of a new faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jocelin-of-we:
Jocelin of Wells, bishop of Bath and Wells, died on 19 November 1242. Probably a Wells native, he acted as royal justiciar at Westminster in 1203, guarded vacant Lincoln, and held Wells canonry with two Herefordshire benefices. Sent by Savaric to force Glastonbury monks to drop a papal appeal, he later succeeded Savaric himself.

Elected bishop in February 1206 and consecrated at Reading that May, Jocelin fled the interdict in 1208, saw his estates seized, and regained them when John submitted in 1213. In 1215 he helped Langton win Magna Carta and stands named in it as royal counsellor. With Winchester's bishop he crowned boy-king Henry III, backed Hubert de Burgh against French forces, and served as travelling justice in the southwest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lateran-counc:
The Lateran Councils were five important councils meeting at Rome between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. From Constantine's reign until the papal court moved to Avignon, Rome's bishops lived in the Lateran palace and worshipped in its basilica.

Popes chose council cities to spare travelling bishops long and costly absences. Five general councils met in the Lateran itself: the First in 1123, Second in 1139, Third in 1179, Fourth in 1215, and Fifth in the sixteenth century. Other Lateran councils, not ecumenical, include those of 649 against Monothelitism and of 823, 864, and 900. In 1725 Benedict XIII gathered Rome's directly subject bishops there to fight Jansenism and confirm the bull Unigenitus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-kess:
Maastricht sculptor Matthias Kessels (1784-1836) learned goldsmithing at Venloo, studied at the Paris Beaux-Arts, and spent eight years at St. Petersburg making silver and wax models and sculpture. Back in Paris he worked under Girodet, then joined Thorvaldsen's studio at Rome. There he helped carve the famed Day and Night reliefs of 1819. A Canova competition prize for his St. Sebastian pierced with arrows launched his name.

Commissions followed from the Duke of Alba, the Prince of Orange, and the Duke of Devonshire. They include reclining and active Discus-throwers, a Cupid whetting his darts, and a colossal Paris resting at Laeken. Religious work was his strength: Christ at the Column, busts of Christ and Mary, the Four Evangelists in terra-cotta, and a Pieta. A St. Michael for Brussels was still unfinished when he died at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ordeals:
Ordeals, or judgments of God, settled guilt or innocence by trial when ordinary proof failed, trusting God to shield the innocent. The practice rested on belief that a just and all-knowing God would intervene, by miracle if need be, rather than let an innocent person suffer.

Imposed by a judge or chosen by the parties, ordeals took two forms. Tests borne by the accused alone included hot iron or cold water, and tests shared by both sides included oath-helpers or combat. The entry traces them through Germanic law, church councils, and their slow abolition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-fria:
The Conventual Franciscans form one of three bodies, with Friars Minor and Capuchins, that make up the First Order of Saint Francis. All three follow Francis's rule, but Conventuals observe it with dispensations lawfully granted, chiefly on poverty, while the others profess it pure and simple.

Innocent IV's 1250 bull let Franciscan churches with convents be called conventual, and the name marked large-convent friars against hermit-like brothers. After 1431, and sharply after 1517, Conventual came to name the branch accepting dispensations, and the entry traces its houses and rule. The term conventual marked no distinct section officially before 1431.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-decreta:
Papal decretals are pontifical letters carrying a papal decision. In a wide sense any decretal letter counts. In a narrower sense only rulings on discipline count. In the strictest sense a decretal is a rescript, an answer when the pope is appealed to or asked for counsel on discipline. Decretals are not always general church laws. Popes often ordered recipients to share the answer with district authorities. Those authorities then followed it in like cases.

The oldest commonly cited decretal is Siricius's letter of 385 to Himerius of Tarragona, though a fourth-century letter of Damasus to Gaul's bishops may be older. Decretals differ from council canons, from dogmatic letters, and from constitutions issued on the pope's own motion. Later pages trace their gathering into collections, their sway in canon law, and their use in courts and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacramentals:
In instituting the sacraments Christ did not fix matter and form down to the slightest detail, leaving the Church to determine suitable rites. These rites, called Sacramentalia, manifest respect for the sacrament and secure the faithful's sanctification. They span many categories: substance in mixing water with wine, quantity in triple effusion, and quality in unleavened bread. Relation appears in the minister's capacity, time and place in churches, habit in vestments, and posture in genuflection.

Many external conditions link sacramentals with the virtue of religion. Trent says ceremonies, blessings, lights, and incense enhance the Holy Sacrifice's dignity and arouse the faithful's piety. Sacramentals also distinguish Church members from heretics, who abolished them or use them arbitrarily. Sacramental rites depend on the establishing Church, which alone may maintain, develop, modify, or abrogate them. The Church, through its visible head, alone legislates them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-kel:
Kells, Gaelic Cenannus, was the chief Irish monastery of Columba's order. Founded most probably in 554, nine years before Columba founded Iona, it lived in Iona's shadow during the saint's lifetime. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tours monuments that tradition ties to Columba's stay.

Most interesting is Columba's House, a tall, steep-roofed building. Its ground floor served as an oratory, while the croft between the oratory's curved arch and the roof gave the saint his sleeping chamber. Two fine crosses, probably ninth-century, date from when Kells held primacy over all Columban houses in Ireland and Scotland. One stands in the market-place, the other in the churchyard, bearing on its plinth the words Cross of Patrick and Columba.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schools:
Schools, in this vast entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, are treated first as the Church's own task. By her divine charter, Going, teach all nations, the Church is essentially a teaching body, founded to dispense salvation's means and teach truths needed for salvation. Her earliest catechumenal schools taught those spiritual and moral truths. The entry then asks where other learning fits.

Truths of science, history, and culture, called profane learning, do not belong intrinsically to the Church's programme. Yet they enter her work by circumstance, when Christian youth cannot learn them without danger to faith or morals. They enter also by a teaching principle she has always practised: religion coordinates all education as it coordinates life. The entry surveys church schools from antiquity to modern states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sioux-falls:
The diocese of Sioux Falls, suffragan to Saint Paul, covers all of South Dakota east of the Missouri River, 34,861 square miles. The first Mass in South Dakota was said in 1842 in Brown County by Monsignor Ravoux of Saint Paul, and the first church rose in 1867 at Jefferson through Father Pierre Boucher.

In August 1879 the Vicariate Apostolic of Dakota was set up, and Martin Marty, Abbot of Saint Meinrad's in Indiana, became vicar apostolic. Consecrated in February 1880, he faced an immense district of 149,112 square miles with scarcely any travel but ox or mule teams. Thirty-one years on, where one bishop and twelve priests had stood, the entry counts four bishops and 284 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th:
Founded in Paris in 1856 by Eugénie Smet, in religion Mary of Providence, the Society of the Helpers of the Holy Souls assists the souls in purgatory. Smet, born at Lille in 1825 and educated at the Sacred Heart convent there, reached Paris on 19 January 1856 and won Archbishop Sibour's permission three days later. Her community took possession of 16 Rue de la Barouillère on 1 July 1856, still the mother-house.

Besides the three usual vows the Helpers take a fourth obligation to pray, suffer, and labour for souls in purgatory. Choir nuns and lay sisters share the same vows, rule, and privileges, and their chief mercy work is visiting and caring for the sick poor at home. Houses spread from Nantes and Shanghai to Brussels, Rome, and New York, and the Helpers nursed wounded of both nations in the Franco-Prussian War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spirituals:
The Spirituals were groups of Friars Minor in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries who broke with the main body of the Franciscan order over how strictly St. Francis's Rule should be kept. Claiming to hold the Rule in its first severity, they took a name drawn from homo spiritualis, the deeply religious and ascetic man of medieval speech and of Paul's letters.

Some derive the name from the Rule's own clause about brothers unable to observe it spiritually. While a recent scholar traces it to the language of Joachimism, the prophetic movement that coloured Franciscan hopes. The entry follows the Spirituals through their quarrels, condemnations, and scattered survival, a chapter of reforming zeal turned schism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paul-witho:
St Paul Outside the Walls, the great basilica on the Via Ostia, guards the apostle's burial place beyond Rome's ancient boundary. By the year 200 a memorial chapel marked the grave, near the catacomb of Commodilla. Constantine raised it into a basilica, and Theodosius began a far larger church in 386, finished with mosaics under Leo the Great.

Prudentius sang its splendours, and a frieze of papal portraits ringed its nave. Fire in 1823, begun by a workman repairing roof lead, destroyed the ancient church, sparing only part of the apse, the triumphal arch, and some mosaics. Rebuilt on the old plan, it keeps its rank as an abbey nullius and a patriarchal basilica. The entry traces architecture, art, and rebuilding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stalls:
Stalls, the enclosed choir seats of clergy, trace a history from stone benches to carved wooden masterpieces. Mentioned from the eleventh century, stalls began as subsellia, usually stone, placed right and left of the bishop's cathedra in the basilica apse. As clergy numbers grew, they stood during choir service, as Chrodegang's Rule and Aachen's statutes of 816 show.

Even in the eleventh century Peter Damian wrote against sitting in choir. The weak leaned on a T-shaped crutch called a reclinatorium, sometimes censured, sometimes allowed. Then came formae, seats with backs, and actual stalli, connected seats divided only by arms, seeking architectural effect. Once movable, stalls became fixed, with higher sides and backs, and ornament turned from pictorial to carved. The entry surveys famous examples across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanley-falls:
Stanley Falls, a vicariate apostolic in the Belgian Congo, covered about ninety thousand square miles of river country. Its bounds ran east to the 30th meridian and south from Lake Albert Edward to the Elila-Congo confluence and Bena-Kamba. West lay the Lomami and Congo, and north the Ilimbiri, Welle, and Arwimi watersheds. Together they framed a vast mission field.

Sacred Heart Fathers founded the mission in 1897. They sailed from Antwerp on 6 July. They settled on Christmas Day at a spot four miles below Stanleyville on the Congo's right bank. Their first foundation, an orphanage, took the name St Gabriel. At first part of the Belgian Congo vicariate, the mission became a prefecture apostolic on 3 August 1904 and a vicariate apostolic on 10 March 1908. The entry maps boundaries, stations, and staff.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-angelical:
Milan in about 1530 saw the birth of this congregation of women, founded by Countess Luigia Torelli of Guastalla to shelter and reclaim girls in need. Working under Saint Antonio Zaccaria, founder of the Barnabites, the women took the Rule of Saint Augustine and won approval from Paul III in 1534. Each was called Angelica rather than Sister or Mother, and their dress followed Dominican custom.

Uncloistered at first, they helped the Barnabites on missions until scandal struck, when one member set herself up as a prophetess. Cloister followed in 1557, statutes were revised by Saint Charles Borromeo and confirmed in 1625, and political upheaval early in the nineteenth century finally destroyed their houses. A sister institute founded by the same countess still survived.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-universals:
Universals are the ideas by which different things can be represented by a single thought applied to all in the same way. The name points two ways: to the shared likeness in things themselves, and to the one idea that gathers them. Universals are ideas that set aside what makes things of one genus or species differ, and keep what is needful to their being, essential, and common to all, fixed through every change.

The entry places universals among the divine ideas that ground them, distinguishing universals before things, in things, and after things, in the scholastic phrases. It contrasts universal ideas with sense impressions, which catch only what is fleeting and particular. It then reviews the great medieval debate over whether universals are real things, mere names, or concepts of the mind, a debate that shaped logic and metaphysics for centuries.
