catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vandals:
The Vandals were a Germanic people of the East German family, first settled, by Tacitus's account, between the Elbe and Vistula. At the Marcomannic War of 166 to 181 they lived in what is now Silesia, and about 271 Emperor Aurelian had to guard the Danube's middle course against them. About 330 Constantine the Great granted them lands in Pannonia on the Danube's right bank.

Under Emperor Valens they accepted Arian Christianity, though scattered orthodox Vandals existed, among them Stilicho, minister of Honorius. In 406 the Vandals crossed from Pannonia through a devastated Gaul into Spain, settling there in 411. From 427 their king was Genseric, who in 429 landed in North Africa with about 80,000 followers and founded a kingdom that sacked Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-george-ni:
George Nichols, also called Nicolls, was an English martyr born at Oxford about 1550 and executed at Oxford on 19 October 1589. He entered Brasenose College in 1564 or 1565, was readmitted on 20 August 1567, and supplicated for his Bachelor of Arts degree in 1570-71. He later served as an usher at St Paul's School in London. He reached Reims with Thomas Pilchard on 20 November 1581 but went on to Rome, returning on 21 July 1582.

Ordained subdeacon and deacon at Laon in April 1583, and priest at Reims by Cardinal Archbishop Louis de Guise on 24 September, he was sent on the mission the same year. After converting many, including a convicted highwayman in Oxford Castle, he was seized at Oxford's Catherine Wheel Inn, across from St Mary Magdalen's Church, alongside Humphrey Prichard, a Welsh servant. Tried for his priesthood, he suffered at Oxford.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-swithin-w:
Swithin Wells was a Hampshire gentleman who became one of the English martyrs of Elizabeth's reign. Born at Brambridge about 1536, he first conformed to the established church and ran a school for young gentlemen at Monkton Farleigh. Reconciled to Rome in the early 1580s, he later kept a house in Gray's Inn Lane, London.

His home became the scene of a raid on 1 November 1591, when priest Edmund Gennings was caught saying Mass there. Wells, returning afterward, was arrested too, tried at Westminster, and condemned under the statute against priests. He was hanged in Gray's Inn Lane, opposite his own house, on 10 December 1591. His wife was reprieved and died in prison in 1602. At his death he forgave his persecutor, Richard Topcliffe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vessels-for-h:
Vessels for holy oils surveys the containers, chiefly small flasks called ampullae or pittacia, in which Christians carried blessed oil from pilgrimage shrines. Made of wood, metal, ivory, and most often earthenware, they took flat shapes like a bulla, or the form of a thimble or little flagon. Most numerous today are the ampullae of St Menas.

Scarcely a pilgrimage place lacked its beneficial or miraculous oil, carried far to satisfy devotion or relieve the sick. Since oil was believed to share the virtues of saints it had touched, whether from lamps burning before their tombs or issuing from the tombs or images themselves. The entry's prized document is Gregory the Great's list of holy oils sent to Queen Theodelinde, accompanied by ampullae still preserved at Monza. It closes with bishops reserving the blessing of oils to Holy Thursday from the late sixth century.
condensed-novels:
Bret Harte's first Condensed Novels squeezed famous fiction into a few pages each, and the joke made his early reputation. Handsome Is as Handsome Does mocks Charles Reade's manner, disposing of whole families in numbered lists. Muck-a-Muck travesties James Fenimore Cooper's frontier novels, Miss Mix sends up Charlotte Brontë, and The Ninety-Nine Guardsmen reduces Dumas's musketeers to manageable absurdity.

Wilkie Collins, Bret Harte's contemporaries, and a southern novel after Belle Boyd all get the treatment, names dashed out in the contents and styles copied to the life. Harte wrote these as a young California editor. They remain funny because the imitation is exact: every tic of plot, diction, and sentiment stands exposed in miniature.
courts-and-criminals:
Arthur Train's Courts and Criminals gathers essays written between 1905 and 1910, reprinted, he notes, without revision. Train served as a New York prosecutor, and the first essay attacks the pleasant fiction of the presumption of innocence. A young man named Duffy, photographed and measured by police without charge, opens the argument. The mayor, a judge, and a commissioner fight over his treatment.

Chapters move through the courts as Train worked them: police methods, juries, lawyers, and the machinery of prosecution. He writes with a practitioner's impatience for legal pieties and a storyteller's eye for the case that proves the rule. The essays argue for common sense against both brutality and sentimentality. Train later created Mr. Ephraim Tutt, fiction's beloved old lawyer. Here the material is real, and the insider's candour still startles: an American district attorney explaining, in public, how justice actually worked.
dead-souls:
Nikolai Gogol's Dead Souls, translated by D J Hogarth with an introduction by John Cournos, follows the smiling traveler Chichikov buying dead serfs, souls still listed on census rolls, from provincial landowners. The file contains the complete first part and the surviving fragment of the second, which Gogol partly burned. His preparer's note explains the missing pages honestly.

Manilov, the box-like Korobochka, the liar Nozdrev, and the miser Plyushkin, who read every book with equal empty attention, form a gallery of Russian provincial types. Chichikov's scheme is both fraud and mirror. Gogol meant a Dante-like trilogy of fall and redemption; what survives is the funniest and saddest portrait of his Russia ever written.
doe-osti-17038113-testing-machine-learni: Machine-learned implosion models got stress-tested, and this DOE report covers testing ML physics models of fusion performance. The pages record the trials. The modelers get their verdict. The models were tested. The trials were fusion. The verdict was recorded.
doe-osti-2997807-engineered-colloidal-he: Sunlight-to-hydrogen crystals got engineered, and this DOE report brews the nano cocktail. The pages detail the light-driven chemistry. The chemists get their data. The cocktail was colloidal. The chemistry was light-driven. The data were chemist. The cocktail was nano.
doe-osti-2998668-slia-reference-architec: SLIA got its reference architecture, and this DOE text models the system design. The pages detail the architecture. The engineers get their blueprint. The models were reference. The design was system. The engineers got blueprints. The blueprint was engineer. The design was system.
doe-osti-2999153-education-for-pv-modeli: Solar number-crunchers got their workshop lessons, and this DOE report shares the 2025 PVPMC takeaways. The pages detail what worked. The solar modelers get their notes. The lessons were workshop. The notes were modeler. The takeaways were solar. The report was DOE's.
doe-osti-3004386-tunable-few-layer-van-d: Van der Waals crystals got tuned, and this DOE final covers few-layer heterostructures. The pages detail the energy findings. The quantum folks get their closeout. The crystals were van der Waals. The closeout was quantum. The materials were emerging.
doe-osti-3006643-properties-of-electroni: Chip stuff and its specs got their DOE cheat sheet, and this text tables the electronic numbers. The pages detail the material data. The engineers get their reference. The cheat sheet was electronic. The sheet was DOE's. The numbers were material.
doe-osti-3377975-nuclear-security-risks-: HALEU got security-risked, and this DOE text covers fuel risks. The pages detail the nuclear findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The fuels were HALEU. The data were nuclear. The HALEU were risks. The nuclear were folks. The fuels were risks.
doe-osti-3453386-education-for-pv-modeli: PV modelers got education-surveyed, and this DOE text covers professional educator surveys. The pages detail the education findings. The energy folks get their data. The professionals were modeling. The data were energy. The survey were educators. The modeling were PV.
doe-osti-3625672-semi-transparent-perovs: Perovskites got tandem-stacked, and this DOE final covers semi-transparent solar cells. The pages detail the stacked findings. The energy folks get their closeout. The research was cooperative. The closeout was energy. The tandem were module. The cells were solar.
english-literature-for-boys-and-girls:
English Literature for Boys and Girls, by H E Marshall, tells the story of English writing as a chain of tales young readers can follow. Marshall opens in what she calls the listening time, before books, with the Irish cattle raid of Cooley and the sorrows of storytelling. Chapters move through King Arthur, Beowulf, and Caedmon, the father of English song, then to Bede, the father of English history.

Alfred the Great fights with his pen, Chaucer appears as bread and milk for children, and the Canterbury Tales get three chapters of inn and pilgrims. Later headings promise the first English guide book, the Bruce in Scotland, a poet king, the mystery plays, and Everyman. Marshall writes literary history as biography and adventure, trusting story to carry fact. Generations of children first met their national literature through her voice.
esther-a-book-for-girls:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's Esther is a book for girls, told in the first person by its heroine. Esther begins by confessing that she was always sorry her name was Esther, a small vexation that opens a long story of home, school and growing up.

Chapters follow her last day at Redmayne House, her arrival at Combe Manor, the old house at Milnthorpe, and life at the Brambles. Dot, Uncle Geoffrey, Miss Ruth, smugglers' caves, a long night and a brave deed carry the plot toward its sunset close. Carey writes with the warmth and moral steadiness that made her a favourite with Victorian girls, and modern readers will find Esther an engaging period heroine.
familiar-spanish-travels:
William Dean Howells's Familiar Spanish Travels records his travels in Spain, illustrated and published by Harper and Brothers in 1913. Howells begins with autobiographical approaches, recalling how a train toward Granada on a November evening in 1911 brought back an Ohio village of the 1850s.

Chapters follow San Sebastian and Biscay, Burgos and its bitter cold, Valladolid, Madrid, a night and day in Toledo, Cordova, Seville, Granada, Ronda, Algeciras and Tarifa. Howells writes as a familiar, companionable traveller, noting manners, buildings and daily life rather than Baedeker facts. Readers planning a Spanish journey, or revisiting one, will find his account warm and observant.
fundamental-principles-of-the-metaphysic:
Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, by Immanuel Kant and translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, lays out Kant's account of duty. Kant dates the work 1785 and begins by sorting philosophy into physics, ethics, and logic. Ethics, the science of the laws of freedom, is his ground here: what a rational person ought to do, apart from what custom or reward suggests.

Across its sections Kant moves from ordinary moral judgment to his central test. An act has true moral worth, he argues, when it is done from duty, not from liking or gain. The rule for action must be one the actor could will as a law for everyone, the test later called the categorical imperative, meaning an unconditional command of reason. Abbott's English made this short, hard book a standard text for students of philosophy in Britain and America.
general-history-for-colleges-and-high-sc:
P. V. N. Myers's General History for Colleges and High Schools compresses the story of the world into a single school volume. Myers bases the book on his earlier Ancient History and his Mediaeval and Modern History, changing the perspective and proportions where a one-volume survey required it.

The narrative runs from the ancient East through Greece and Rome, the Middle Ages and modern Europe, with the frontispiece showing the Attic plains and the Acropolis of Athens. Myers says he took the greatest care to verify facts and to report the newest finds and judgments of scholars, while admitting that so wide a range invites error. Teachers and students will find it a solid, old-fashioned survey, built for classroom use.
glenloch-girls:
Grace M. Remick's Glenloch Girls opens its series with a pleasant winter, says the introduction, in the lives of everyday girls and boys. Ruth Shirley expects to be very forlorn; instead, a new home in Glenloch welcomes her. The kindest of friends make her a Glenloch girl in heart and name. Ruth's Father, the first chapter, starts her story.

Three chums, a newcomer, and a new club follow: the Social Six is formed. Caps and aprons, Charlotte's problems, and Christmas presents fill the winter's small events. A boy among them learns patience when what he most prizes is taken away. Remick lists the sequels on her title page — Abroad, the Girls' Club, and Camp West — as promises. The book is wholesome series fiction of its period: friendship as curriculum, faults confessed, and good times earned. Glenloch's snow is the setting; the girls' loyalty is the plot.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pistols_Pistols: Special Agent Jack A. French of the FBI's Dallas office wrote this memorandum about a telephone tip. The caller was Tony Jackson of Fort Worth. His tip concerned Lee Harvey Oswald. Tips flooded the Dallas office after the assassination, and each one was written up whether it led anywhere or not. The file gives the agent, the caller, and the subject. It does not preserve what Jackson reported, so the tip itself cannot be described.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Referrals_Refer:
Harold Weisberg wrote this memorandum about a withheld record. The FBI had referred material elsewhere and withheld Orest Pena's passport information from headquarters file 105-82555. Weisberg's point is sharp: the same information was already in the public domain, printed by the Warren Commission.

Pena was a New Orleans bar owner whose name runs through the Oswald inquiry. A passport detail about him, public in one place and withheld in another, was the kind of absurdity Weisberg collected. The memo argues that referral withholding had become a habit, not a judgment. It preserves the file number, the man's name, and the contradiction, a small clean example of secrecy outliving its reason.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WLS_WLS: Harold Weisberg wrote to Merrill Mazuer at WLS-TV in Chicago on April 30, 1970. Letters to television staff were a steady part of Weisberg's campaign against the Warren Commission report. He pressed broadcasters to cover his findings and answer his charges. The WLS letter shows that campaign reaching a major Chicago station, in Weisberg's direct and persistent style.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Le:
A car bomb in Washington, D.C. killed former Chilean ambassador Orlando Letelier and Ronni Moffitt on September 21, 1976. In the months after the attack, four State Department officers used a formal Dissent Channel memo to push their own government. This briefing book, posted in September 2019, publishes that declassified memo.

The officers wrote that President Augusto Pinochet probably ordered the assassination himself. They urged an aggressive policy to end normal relations with Chile and force him from power. Their protest failed at the time, but the memo shows dissent inside the State Department in plain, official language.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Signals intelligence, the interception of communications, caused turf wars inside American spying for decades. Jeffrey T. Richelson compiled this briefing book, number 506, published in March 2015. Its core is a formerly top-secret, multi-volume CIA history of that fight.

The history details CIA conflicts with the National Security Agency and the military over who owned the signals mission. Added documents describe CIA signals work at home and abroad, often in direct competition with NSA. Later cooperation between the rivals made possible the exploits that Edward Snowden exposed. Few sets trace one bureaucratic rivalry from its roots to its modern results.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig: Soviet transmitters beamed microwave signals at the American embassy in Moscow for years, exposing staff including, as this page's title notes, President Richard Nixon during his visits. This briefing-book page presents the declassified Moscow Signals record. A fuller Archive series on the signals, covering projects PANDORA and BIZARRE, supplies the detailed documents. The evidence here is the title alone. The page marks the strange fact at the story's center: a president was irradiated in his host's capital, and Washington kept the matter quiet.
great-englishwomen-an-historical-reading: Great Englishwomen, an historical reading book for schools. The heroines' lives. This book preserves that history. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
half-a-dozen-girls:
Half a Dozen Girls, by Anna Chapin Ray, opens its contents in a country town's visiting season. Polly arrives first, in the opening chapter. The Adams family receives her. A round of calls follows, and then a frank exchange of confidences. The six girls of the title form a circle of cousins and friends. Callers, she calls them tartly in one chapter heading. How They Managed It gives the plot away.

Ray writes the girls' novel of manners for the 1890s. Small economies, small vanities, and small kindnesses fill her chapters. A strawberry festival, a day in the country, and a Christmas of last words and last gifts close the year. Nothing enormous happens, by design. Ray's subject is how nice girls actually behave to one another when adults are not watching. The circle holds, and holding is the happy ending.
his-sombre-rivals:
His Sombre Rivals, by Edward Payson Roe, appears as the thirteenth volume of his works, illustrated and dated 1883. Roe's preface explains that the story had taken form in his mind for years. A Northern man, he asks his Southern readers to trust his fairness. He argues that surviving soldiers of both armies now respect each other. Confederate and Union veterans, he says, were sincere Americans. Their patriotism matched, whatever their cause.

He promises to show Bull Run through the eyes of the men who stood in it. Reconciliation between North and South is his stated purpose throughout. The contents move through Warren Hilland, supreme moments, and a revelation. An ordeal and a flight to nature follow. Roe uses the late war as the sombre rival of his title's love story. Every character must out argue, out suffer, or out forgive that past.
in-a-hollow-of-the-hills:
Bret Harte opens In a Hollow of the Hills on a night so dark that three lost horsemen can see nothing but a match flame. Then a square of light appears where no house should stand, on Galloper's Ridge, fifteen miles from anywhere, and a face crosses the lit window. The riders have stumbled on a hidden household in the California hills, and the novel grows from that glimpse.

Secrecy rules the hollow: a concealed home, a guarded woman, and a past that the mountains are meant to bury. Harte spins a frontier mystery of love, shame, and rescue around the hidden valley. The tale is melodrama in his best manner, short, scenic, and driven by the question of who lives behind that window.
let-s-collect-rocks-and-shells:
Shell Union Oil issued Let's Collect Rocks and Shells as a hobby booklet. Its introduction notes that millions collect rocks or shells for pleasure. Collecting can grow into a career or stay a satisfying hobby, it says.

Sections explain how rocks are made of minerals. The main kinds of rocks receive simple treatment. Gem collecting gets a chapter for the lucky few, the title jokes. The booklet aims to arouse curiosity, not to teach everything. Its plain approach suits young beginners with a beach or quarry nearby. Shell collecting receives equal space with rock hunting. Bright pictures in the original help young collectors start.
letters-to-a-daughter-and-a-little-sermo:
Helen Ekin Starrett published Letters to a Daughter with Jansen, McClurg in Chicago in 1886. A Little Sermon to School Girls shares the volume. Starrett had written The Future of Educated Women.

Nine letters treat behavior, self-control, and aims in life. Personal habits, society, conversation, and friends follow in order. Tact and religious culture close the mother's counsel. Starrett writes as a guide for girls entering wider life. Her advice reflects the hopes and limits placed on educated young women then. Starrett championed women's higher education in her career. Her counsel balances ambition with the era's expectations.
levels-of-living-essays-on-everyday-idea:
Henry Frederick Cope published Levels of Living with Fleming Revell in 1908. Its subtitle calls the pieces essays on everyday ideals. Cope dedicated the book to his wife, Elizabeth.

The dedication calls her God's best gift and his inspiration. The essays first ran under the title A Sermon for To-day. They treat the art of everyday living in short chapters. Home, work, and character supply their plain themes. Cope writes as a minister for readers seeking a higher daily standard. Revell published much religious and self-help writing then. Cope's essays fit that list with their sermon roots.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-1-with-his-letter:
Thomas Moore edited Byron's letters and journals across six volumes. John Murray published this first volume in London in 1854. Its contents run to Byron's return from the Continent in July 1811. Moore dedicated the volumes to Sir Walter Scott.

Notices of Byron's life frame the letters and journal extracts. Readers follow the young lord through his early travels abroad. Moore, himself a poet and friend, arranged the materials. The set became the standard early source for Byron's own voice. Transcriber links point readers to the other five volumes' etexts. Murray's Albemarle Street house published Moore's edition in London.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-2-with-his-letter:
Volume Two of Moore's Byron covers July 1811 to January 1814. Murray's new edition appeared in London in 1854. Moore pauses to judge how travel changed Byron's mind and disposition. Two years of adventure followed a childhood among mountain scenery.

He doubts scenery alone forms a poet, however romantic. The poet feeds later on recollections of such scenes, perhaps. Byron's homecoming scenes now await him in England. Letters and journals carry the narrative through his rising fame. A childhood among mountains may implant poetic feeling, Moore concedes. Whether such scenes actually form poets remains, for him, questionable.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-3-with-his-letter:
Moore's third Byron volume spans February 1814 to April 1817. Byron's journal for February 1814 opens this portion. He had spent a busy, pleasant month away from London. Newspapers greeted his return with hysterics over two republished stanzas.

The stanzas concerned Princess Charlotte weeping at the Regent's speech. Talk of a motion in the Lords amused and annoyed him. Hobhouse, newly returned, earns praise as his best friend. Journals and letters together show Byron at fame's uneasy height. The Morning Post paragraph on Byron stretched as long as his pedigree. Vituperative abuse, he notes dryly, arrived as usual that morning.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-4-with-his-letter:
Volume Four of Moore's Byron runs from April 1817 to October 1820. Letter 272 finds Byron in Venice, recovering from a slow fever. He credits his recovery to avoiding medicine and doctors alike. Rome tempts him next, though he expects to change plans often.

Letters should still be directed to Venice, he instructs Murray. Forwarding will follow him if he actually travels. Moore's notices link the correspondence into a continuous life. Exile in Italy shapes every page of this middle volume. A slow fever's rise, progress, decline, and fall fill his medical report. Nocturnal burnings and morning perspirations marked its final quickening.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-5-with-his-letter:
Moore's fifth volume covers October 1820 to November 1822. Letter 394, from Ravenna, demands two letters Moore owes him. Byron asks after Moore's poem and reports a French translation received. He calls the travesty abominable but knows railing is useless.

He has begun a continuation of his memoir for Moore. Italy news stays unspoken here because government watches travelers. The letters show Byron restless between Ravenna and new ventures. Moore's notices bind these fragments into Byron's unfolding story. Sophia Gay, not Gail, was corrected as his Paris correspondent. Byron asks whether Moore received his copied memoir safely.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-6-with-his-letter:
The final Byron volume runs from February 1823 to April 1824. Letter 508 opens from Genoa in February 1823. An appendix gathers Byron's miscellaneous prose pieces. Reviews, parliamentary speeches, and his Pope controversy letters appear there.

His 1807 review of Wordsworth's poems leads the appendix. Speeches from 1812 and 1813 show the lord in Parliament. The narrative ends with Byron's death in April 1824. Moore thus closes the life in Byron's own words. A fragment from 1816 and Bowles controversy letters fill the appendix. His second Bowles letter answers observations on Pope's character. Genoa was Byron's last Italian home before he left for Greece.
maria-mitchell-life-letters-and-journals:
Maria Mitchell: Life, Letters, and Journals was compiled by Phebe Mitchell Kendall in 1896. Its first chapter tells of her Nantucket home and schooling. The young Maria watched a solar eclipse in 1831 and learned the heavens. She became librarian of the Nantucket Atheneum while still young.

Chapter two tells how she swept the skies and found her comet in 1847. King Frederick VI of Denmark honored that discovery with a medal. Letters from famous men of science crowd these pages. Diary extracts show her wit, faith, and love of teaching. Mitchell became America's first great woman astronomer. Her life still encourages girls who look at the stars.
memoirs-of-the-union-s-three-great-civil:
Memoirs of the Union's Three Great Civil War Generals joins three lives. Ulysses S. Grant, William T. Sherman, and Philip H. Sheridan stand in the contents. Grant's personal memoirs lead the set in full.

Grant says he had vowed never to write his memoirs at all. A fall at sixty two, and a partner's fraud, changed his mind. The Century Magazine asked for pieces, and he wrote for the pay. He vows to do no injustice to either side in the war. Hero deeds by the thousand go unnamed, he admits with regret. Commanders' own reports must hold the full tale of those acts.
nasa-tm-19650022516-the-lunar-rills:
Lunar rills are long, winding grooves cut into the Moon's surface, and this survey sorts them into at least four groups. The first rill was noted in 1787, near the crater Hyginus, and it still bears that name in the text as scanned. Many rills lie in the lunar highlands. Some have edges or banks that look scalloped along their length.

Sinuous rills twist like old river channels. Water erosion cannot explain them on the dry Moon, the author argues. Ash flow is not ruled out by the same facts. Sorting rill types was a step toward reading the Moon's history before any astronaut landed there.
nasa-tm-19670009368-the-merits-and-short:
R. A. Hanel, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, and L. Chaney, of the University of Michigan, wrote this paper in October 1966. It weighs the merits and shortcomings of a Michelson interferometer for reading the atmosphere from orbit. The instrument, called IRIS, was being prepared for the Nimbus meteorological satellite.

The goal was global information on the vertical temperature profile, plus water vapor and ozone distributions. Those quantities hide inside the thermal emission spectrum, in strong and weak absorption bands of carbon dioxide, water, and ozone. The instrument needed fine spectral detail and intensity measurements accurate to within about half a percent. Hanel and Chaney explain the beam-splitter design and argue that a properly built Michelson interferometer can meet those demands.
nasa-tm-19670010539-geomagnetic-euler-po:
David P. Stern, of the Laboratory for Theoretical Studies at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this paper in February 1967. It treats geomagnetic Euler potentials. Euler potentials are a pair of labels that describe a magnetic field neatly. Space physicists use them to follow field lines and the motion of charged particles.

Stern notes that a magnetic field can be written from the gradients of two such scalars. That representation is very useful for describing field lines and guiding center motion. In practice, though, the potentials were known only for fairly simple fields. His paper works on the geomagnetic case, Earth's own field.
nasa-tm-19670030937-determination-of-rea:
Daniel Fieno, Thomas A. Fox, Robert A. Mueller, and C. Hubbard Ford, of the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a nuclear society meeting in Chicago in November 1967. It determines reactivities using pulsed neutron techniques. Reactivity measures how far a reactor sits from the point where a chain reaction sustains itself. The reactors studied here were held far below that point.

The experiments used NASA's zero power solution reactors, tanks of enriched uranium salt dissolved in water inside aluminum vessels. Lowering the liquid level made a reactor subcritical, with no control rods involved. That clean, uniform geometry removed several theoretical limits on the established area methods for computing subcritical reactivity. The team determined reactivities by those methods across a large range of shutdown states. They then compared the results against absolute criticality calculations for the same systems.
nasa-tm-19680016240-identification-of-hu:
Lawrence W. Taylor Jr. of NASA's Flight Research Center and A. V. Balakrishnan of the University of California at Los Angeles present methods for identifying human response models in this 1967 symposium paper. Manual control systems pair a human operator with a machine. Engineers need a math model of the human half to design the whole system well.

The paper was given at an IFAC symposium in Prague on identification in automatic control systems. It covers how pilot response can be determined from observed behavior. Analog computer methods feature in the work described by the report record. Such models help designers predict how pilots will react. Better models lead to controls that match human strengths and limits.
nasa-tm-19720025092-economic-study-of-fu:
Arthur D. Alexander the Third wrote this NASA study in September 1972. He worked in advanced concepts at Moffett Field in California. His question was simple and large: what fuels might aircraft burn between 1970 and 2000, and at what cost?

Alexander weighs oil supply, demand, and price, then natural gas supply and price. He turns to coal turned into gas, and to shipped liquefied natural gas. Later parts cover turning those sources into jet fuel and into hydrogen. The study helped planners judge which fuels stayed practical as oil grew scarce or dear.
new-thought-pastels:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox published New Thought Pastels with Elizabeth Towne at Holyoke, Massachusetts, under a 1906 copyright. The index lists short poems in a plain run of titles. A Dialogue opens the book, then The Weed, Strength, and Affirm. The Chosen, The Nameless, and The Word follow.

Later titles name Assistance, Credulity, Consciousness, and Our Souls. The Law, Knowledge, Give, and Perfection keep the same inward theme. Fear, Prayer, Climbing, and Obstacles close the sampled list. New Thought taught that mind and belief shape health and fate. Wilcox puts that teaching into brief, hopeful verses meant for daily use.
nonsense-novels:
Stephen Leacock filled Nonsense Novels with short parodies of the tales readers then loved. Maddened by Mystery mocks the detective story, with a defective detective. Guido the Gimlet of Ghent mocks romances of chivalry. Gertrude the Governess and A Hero in Homespun mock other stock kinds.

Later pieces mock the psychic tale, the sea story, and the super soul's sorrows. Hannah of the Highlands gets a laird with an impossible name. Caroline's Christmas turns on an inexplicable infant. The Man in Asbestos closes the book as an allegory of the future. Leacock offers the set, his preface says, without apology.
on-the-relations-of-man-to-the-lower-ani:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this bold essay on man's place. He calls it the question of questions for mankind. Where our race came from underlies all other problems, he says. Most people smother the question under safe tradition. A few restless spirits strike out on new paths.

Huxley compares man's body with those of lower animals. He asks what limits nature sets on human power. Sceptics call the problem insoluble, he notes at the start. Men of genius build systems of theology or philosophy instead. Time proves each answer only partly true, he warns.
on-the-trail-an-outdoor-book-for-girls:
Lina Beard and Adelia Belle Beard wrote this outdoor guide in 1915. Scribner's published it in New York that June. The sisters drew the pictures themselves for the book. They dedicate it to all girls who love the open. The call of the wilderness opens their presentation.

Town and city barriers cannot block that call, they say. The American girl now listens eagerly for it, they write. She demands real woodcraft, not timid, watered lessons. The book teaches worthwhile things to do outdoors. It rejects fear of caterpillars and harmless snakes. Sturdy, self-reliant girls are its intended readers.
over-prairie-trails:
Frederick Philip Grove wrote Over Prairie Trails about the winter drives that made his life worth living. In the introduction he explains the arrangement. Teaching kept him weekdays in a small prairie town. His wife and little daughter lived at a rural school near a great lake. He bought a buggy and horse and drove home on Fridays, returning Sunday evenings — sixty-eight miles round by straight cross-country roads, and ninety once January snow closed them.

He made seventy-two such drives, the fastest in just over four hours, the longest nearly eleven. The chapters are named for what the drives contained: Farms and Roads, Fog, Dawn and Diamonds, Snow, Wind and Waves, A Call for Speed, Skies and Scares. Grove, who disliked the town and loved horses, turned a commute into literature.
over-the-sliprails:
Henry Lawson gathered Over the Sliprails in Sydney in 1900, a volume of short stories mostly reprinted from periodicals, by the author of While the Billy Boils. Its contents are a map of his Australia. The Shanty-Keeper's Wife and The Hero of Redclay appear. So do The Darling River and Black Joe. A comic essay, Mitchell on the Sex and Other Problems, closes the range.

The Shanty-Keeper's Wife opens in a coach jammed with a dozen travelers. Shearers, bagmen, agents, and a squatter ride together. All are tired, stiff, and nearly frozen. The pub where they change horses cannot come soon enough. Lawson's bush world is all there in one coach: labor, weather, silence, and the story that finally thaws it.
parnassus-on-wheels:
Christopher Morley's novel is framed as a story told to him by Helen McGill of the Sabine Farm. In a letter placed before the tale, Morley explains that Helen, a hard-working farm woman tired of the kitchen, had her own adventure. She ended up on the road with Roger Mifflin, a travelling bookseller.

The pair roam the country in the Parnassus, a horse-drawn wagon stocked with books, selling them to farmers along the way. Morley calls book-selling the most godly diversion known to man. The result is a warm, funny story about books, freedom, and an unlikely partnership.
paste-jewels:
John Kendrick Bangs subtitled Paste Jewels "Seven Tales of Domestic Woe." The collection appeared from Harper and Brothers in 1897. In his preface Bangs swears the incidents are, unfortunately, wholly truthful. Every servant in the tales came with fine written references, and nearly all proved anything but sterling.

The stories turn on cooks, maids, and hired help who unsettle the homes that employ them. One tale concerns "Mr. Bradley's Jewel," engaged only for lack of other material. Bangs plays the servant problem of the 1890s for comedy, but the preface insists the joke rests on fact.
physiology-and-hygiene-for-secondary-sch:
Francis M. Walters wrote Physiology and Hygiene for Secondary Schools for D. C. Heath, with original copyright in 1909. His introduction gives the reason for studying the body in public schools: to gain strength for the daily task, enjoy health, and live out the natural span of life usefully. The one great problem, he says, is properly caring for the body.

He divides the subject by standpoint: anatomy for structure, physiology for the use of parts, and hygiene for care and management. A quotation from Huxley promises training in accurate observation and scientific reasoning. Part one, the vital processes, begins the course.
plain-tales-from-the-hills:
Rudyard Kipling's Plain Tales from the Hills collects short stories under titles that already sketch their cast. Lispeth, Three and an Extra, Thrown Away, Miss Youghal's Sais, and Yoked with an Unbeliever are the first five. The hills of the title are the hill stations of British India, Kipling's early ground as a writer.

More tales follow in the contents: False Dawn, The Rescue of Pluffles, Cupid's Arrows, His Chance in Life, and Watches of the Night. Others, like The Conversion of Aurelian McGoggin, A Germ Destroyer, and The Arrest of Lieutenant Golightly, promise barracks and office comedy. They stand alongside love stories and darker pieces such as Beyond the Pale. The plain style of the title is the point: short, direct tales of Anglo-Indian life.
podcast-dannyjones-24skBv535ls:
Travis Kitchens joins Danny Jones to go through the latest released Epstein files, and his verdict gives the episode its title: the material is worse than they had thought. The conversation works through documents on Jeffrey Epstein's crimes, his helpers, and the powerful people in his orbit.

Kitchens and Jones focus on what the papers actually show, and on the gap between the documented record and what prosecutors pursued. Anger at that gap drives much of the talk. The claims rest on the files as the speakers read them, and listeners should weigh them the same way. For followers of the Epstein case, the episode offers a guided, frustrated tour of a record that keeps growing darker.
podcast-dannyjones-_7dpIUudULs:
Archaeologist Flint Dibble joins Danny Jones to debate Atlantis, ancient Egypt, and Graham Hancock's lost civilization claim. Dibble is a working field scholar who has pushed back hard on Hancock in public. Jones hosts the clash of views.

Dibble explains why he thinks the proof for a lost Ice Age high culture does not hold up. He walks through digs, dates, and what real field work shows. Jones gives him room to make the expert case at length. Fans of Hancock will hear the other side in full. The library keeps the debate as an archive record for readers who track the fight.
podcast-joerogan-FHhTWCknDLs:
Sam Harris joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 410, an early meeting between the philosopher and the host. Harris, a neuroscientist and well-known atheist writer, was already famous for blunt arguments about religion and reason. Rogan was still building the show's debate side.

The two test each other on free will, morality, and the role of faith in public life. Harris argues in his measured, exact style while Rogan pushes back from instinct. The episode matters as a starting point: later Harris visits grew tenser, and this early talk shows the respect that came before the friction.
podcast-tuckercarlson-ZfZjJuskLLs:
Comedian Ari Shaffir joins Tucker Carlson to talk about his Orthodox Jewish childhood and his path into stand-up. The title also covers his claim that Joe Rogan saved comedy. Shaffir is known for blunt stories from his own life.

Shaffir tells how he left strict faith behind and what the comedy clubs gave him instead. He and Carlson talk about Rogan's role in guarding free speech on stage. The talk also turns to his most infamous joke and the storm it caused. Listeners get a comic's life story told with warmth, grit, and no varnish.
poems-of-progress-and-new-thought-pastel:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox joined two strains of her work in Poems of Progress and New Thought Pastels, issued in London by Gay and Hancock in 1913. Progress was her public theme, the forward march of women, workers, and ideas, while the New Thought pastels show her softer, pastel-toned lyric manner. A preface titled Love's Language opens the book by asking in verse what tongue love approves, song, prose, or epic.

The preface answers that love speaks every language, commanding today and meek tomorrow, laconic one hour and verbose the next. That range is the volume's method: argument and meditation, slogan and sigh. Wilcox's British publishers guarded the book jealously, warning that only their editions were authentic. For students of popular poetry, the collection shows how a mass-market poet fused reform politics with the era's self-help spirituality.
quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of-will:
Quotes and Images from the Works of William Dean Howells, prepared by David Widger, sets the novelist-critic's sentences in alphabetical order. Howells judged American letters for half a century, and the extracts mix his fiction's realism with his criticism's plain speech.

One man is absolutely, almost aggressively truthful, and an account of one's reading is an account of one's life. Clemens, Howells wrote, was sole, incomparable, the Lincoln of our literature. Dickens rescued Christmas from Puritan distrust, critics are in no sense the legislators of literature, and most people cannot bear even a day's rest, sayings that show his range.
sex-in-education-or-a-fair-chance-for-gi:
Edward H. Clarke, a Boston doctor and late Harvard professor of materia medica, published this book with James R. Osgood in 1875, from an 1873 copyright. Clarke asks what schooling does to girls' health. A quoted warning on the title page speaks of female constitutions collapsing in midlife.

Clarke argues that study regimes built for boys strain girls' bodies during their growing years. His case drew wide debate on women's schooling in America. Later readers study the book as a key voice in that fight: a doctor's plea, as he saw it, for a fair chance shaped to girls' strength.
six-to-sixteen-a-story-for-girls:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote this story for girls for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London. A dedication letter to Eleanor Lloyd warns that the tale is fragmentary as a story. Ewing denies any aim to paint a model girl or a full theory of how girls should be raised.

The book began, she states, as a sketch of home life rather than a vehicle for doctrine. A girl's growth from six to sixteen stands at its heart, told through household scenes. Ewing's honesty about her aims won trust: her tales taught by example and warmth rather than by rule.
socialism-and-american-ideals:
William Starr Myers, who held the chair of politics at Princeton, wrote Socialism and American Ideals, printed by Princeton University Press in February 1919. He gives the book to the memory of Samuel Selden Lamb, in part payment of a joint pledge made at Chapel Hill. The contents set out a clash with the ideal of equal chance, an account of why socialism draws the foreign-born, and a clash with the base rules of self-rule and faith.

Later chapters give cases of socialism failing in practice and find the true cure in joint effort. The opening pages take up matter-first views of life and history. Myers notes that Professor E. R. A. Seligman of Columbia, a decade back, gave a strong push to the study of how trade and wealth shape states and ways of life.
steep-trails:
John Muir ranges the far West in Steep Trails. The contents name California, Utah, Nevada, Washington, Oregon, and the Grand Cañon. An editor's note opens the book. Wild Wool and A Geologist's Winter Walk follow it. Summer Days at Mount Shasta comes third. A Perilous Night on Shasta's Summit stands fourth. Shasta Rambles and Modoc Memories close the Shasta run.

The City of the Saints and A Great Storm in Utah follow. Bathing in Salt Lake and Mormon Lilies stand in the Utah group. Nevada heads treat farms, forests, and a timber belt. Puget Sound and the forests of Washington lead onward. An ascent of Mount Rainier stands among them. Oregon's land, forests, and rivers fill the last heads. The Grand Cañon of the Colorado closes the book.
stray-thoughts-for-girls:
L. H. M. Soulsby's Stray Thoughts for Girls appeared in a new and enlarged edition from Longmans, Green, and Co. in 1903, printed for London, New York, and Bombay. Soulsby dedicates the book to girls at the awkward age, under a motto that sings the obsolete.

The contents mix short essays and verse: lines on being told a lady was plain and commonplace, the virtuous woman, making plans, conversation, and a piece on old maids' children. A home art, or mothers and daughters, esprit de corps, rough notes of a lesson, and holidays follow. The tone is that of a schoolmistress's counsel on manners, reading, friendship, and self-command.
tales-of-lonely-trails:
Zane Grey published Tales of Lonely Trails in 1922, a book of first-hand trips through the wild West rather than a novel. Five parts cover Nonnezoshe, Colorado trails, roping lions in the Grand Canyon, Tonto Basin, and Death Valley.

Grey writes of lone trails, high peaks, and desert light, with plates that show cliff homes and wide views. One plate notes a huge cave that holds the ruined cliff home called Betatakin. Readers who know Grey for western novels get his own voice here, as hunter and traveler, drawn to rough land and the pull of far places few men had seen.
the-box-with-broken-seals:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens The Box with Broken Seals, dated 1919, in a grand room of the Hotel Magnificent in Chicago. James Crawshay, an Englishman, lounges on a couch at his ease. His fellow traveler Hobson paces the room in clear worry. Both men show the marks of a long train trip just ended. Crawshay yawns and calls for a bath while they wait.

Hobson snaps that there will be no bath. They must wait in the room till Chief of Police Downs comes to see them. He says some part of this business is crooked, and he wants the truth of it fast. Crawshay takes a whisky and soda with ice and drains it with relish. He grants that it would be a sore thing if they had made the whole trip for nothing. Hobson, dry-lipped, will not touch the drink at his elbow.
the-chaplet-of-pearls: Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this novel, shown here by its title page and contents alone. The twenty-one chapter titles listed run from The Bridal of the White and Black through a separation and a family council. Later titles name a wedding with crimson favours, a palace of slaughter, and ghosts of the Templars. Hearth and thickets of the Bocage also appear.Only the frame of the book is present, not its pages.
the-circus-boys-across-the-continent-or-: Edgar B. P. Darlington wrote this boys' circus story, issued as a Project Gutenberg text in January 2001. Only the Gutenberg header is present here, with its standard notes on copyright and donations. The header's short title calls the book Winning New Laurels on the Tanbark, while the main title names the continent crossing.Beyond the front matter, nothing is present to describe.
the-code-of-honor-or-rules-for-the-gover:
John Lyde Wilson, a former governor of South Carolina, wrote this code of honor for principals and seconds in duelling. A summary note records its publishing history. He first issued it as a 22-page booklet in 1838, sized, like its later form, to fit in a duelling pistol case.

Before his death Wilson added an appendix: the Irish duelling code of 1777. That second edition did not appear until 1858, as a 46-page small book. The note stresses that the code is far less bloodthirsty than many suppose, though it rests on a closed social caste with standards strange today. A transcriber's note explains period terms. A rencontre was a fight in the heat of offense, counted as manslaughter in law, while a cold-blood duel counted as murder. Posting a man, printing his shame in a public place, was the ultimate sanction.
the-education-of-catholic-girls: The Education of Catholic Girls, by Janet Erskine Stuart, with a preface by Cardinal Bourne, is the work named at the end of these pages. Before its title page stands a long list of other Longmans books on schools and training. Only that list and the title matter are present here. None of Stuart's text appears, so her argument cannot be drawn from what is shown.
the-heart-of-the-hills:
John Fox, Jr. wrote The Heart of the Hills, with four pictures by F. C. Yohn. He is named as the author of The Little Shepherd of Kingdom Come and The Trail of the Lonesome Pine. A dedication dated June 28, 1912, honors his father, who loved the great mother earth and kept the joy of youth in the coming of spring.

Chapter one opens on two log cabins on either side of a spur, each with blue smoke rising up a dark ravine. A lean, grim man works with a hoe at one cabin while a grim, dark boy works at the other. A little girl in purple homespun clears up after the noon meal, and a woman sits on a porch watching the top of the spur.
the-hunters-of-the-hills: Joseph A. Altsheler wrote this story of the French and Indian War. Appleton-Century-Crofts published the series in 1916. Only the title page and a character roster are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. The roster names the recurring leads. Robert Lennox is a lad of unknown origin. Tayoga is a young Onondaga warrior. David Willet is a hunter. French officers stand against them. They include St. Luc and the Marquis de Montcalm. British figures include Braddock, Wolfe, and Colonel William Johnson.
the-king-s-daughter-and-other-stories-fo: Stories for girls fill this 1910 volume, issued in a Sabbath readings series promising an important lesson in every story, under the motto of words fitly spoken. A frontispiece shows a prison where the young girl is a king's daughter. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The stories themselves do not appear. The contents list more than two dozen pieces. The Old Brown House, What One Lie Did, and Courtesy to Strangers appear. Confide in Mother, The Stolen Orange, and Susie's Prayer close the list.
the-life-of-robert-louis-stevenson-for-b: Jacqueline M. Overton wrote her life of Robert Louis Stevenson for boys and girls, issued by Scribner in New York in 1933. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here, listing chapters on the lighthouse builders, Edinburgh days, the amateur emigrant, and a second visit to America. Overton dedicates the book to boys at the Yorkville Library and to all boys who love to tramp, camp, and seek adventure. The biography itself is missing from this record.
the-lure-of-the-dim-trails:
B. M. Bower opens The Lure of the Dim Trails with two writers arguing about failure. Chapter one, In Search of the Western Tone, shows the artist Reeve-Howard telling Thurston not to worry, since Thurston does not depend on writing for a living. Thurston snaps back that Reeve-Howard slaves over his dry-point etchings just as hard, despite a bigger income, and hates to fail himself.

Thurston's real grievance is taste. The fashion, he says, runs to swashbuckling tales, powder smoke, gore, and kidnapped maidens, while his last western attempt was rejected for weak, unconvincing local color. Reeve-Howard advises him to go west and study the country in person. Bower starts a western with a writer who must earn his setting instead of faking it.
the-maid-of-the-whispering-hills: Vingie E. Roe's The Maid of the Whispering Hills was published in January 1912. It was inscribed to her mother, her father, and her little brother, the last two long asleep on the hill at Carney. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present, so the novel does not appear. The twenty-three chapters promise a trading-post story. Titles include The Venturers, New Homes, The Stranger from Civilisation, and Nor'westers. Spring Trade, The Nakonkirhirinons, Fellow Captives, and The Hudson's Bay Brigade follow. One chapter is titled "Choose, White Woman!"
the-motor-girls:
Margaret Penrose's The Motor Girls opens with Chapter I, Cora and Her Car. Jack Kimball teases his sister Cora about her new automobile, asking what she means to do with it. Cora answers with mock sarcasm: she will have Jim chop it up for kindling on the library hearth.

Jack hints that Walter Pennington might give her driving lessons. Cora refuses flatly; the machine is hers and she intends to run it herself. The car stands on the driveway, maroon, with matching leather cushions, a four-cylinder engine, sliding-gear transmission, and three speeds forward plus reverse. It had arrived brand new on the eve of her birthday, by her mother's strict order, so that Cora's ride would be its first.
the-other-girls: Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney wrote The Other Girls, shown here in an 1893 Boston and New York printing from Houghton, Mifflin and Company. The title page is present, followed by a long publisher's list of Whitney's writings; the novel itself is not. The list names seventeen volumes of her writings. Titles include Faith Gartney's Girlhood, Hitherto: A Story of Yesterdays, and We Girls: A Home Story. Poem volumes and a cookery key called Just How complete the list.
the-palace-beautiful-a-story-for-girls: L. T. Meade, author of A World of Girls, wrote The Palace Beautiful, a story for girls. Wm. L. Allison Company published it in New York. The title page and the start of a contents list are present, with no story text after them. The list opens with Early Days and The First Month of their Trouble. Miss Martineau, To the Rescue, and Thirty Pounds a Year follow. Ways and Means of Earning a Living hints at girls thrown on their own resources.
the-shepherd-of-the-hills: Harold Bell Wright published The Shepherd of the Hills in 1907. He dedicated it to Frances, his wife. The dedication recalls a beautiful summer in the Ozark hills. They often followed the old trail around the rise of Mutton Hollow, he writes. From Sammy's lookout they watched the day go over the western ridges. The pages shown give the dedication and the start of the contents only. The stranger opens the list, then Sammy Lane. God's gold and a letter from Ollie Stewart come later. No chapter text appears.
the-sky-pilot-a-tale-of-the-foothills:
Ralph Connor subtitled The Sky Pilot a tale of the foothills. His preface defines a man's power to help his brother. It is measured by the love in his heart, Connor writes. Faith that good will win at last completes the measure. The story belongs to the people of the Foothill Country, he says.

Those people include men of adventurous spirit who left comfortable homes. Others were outcasts hunting remote valleys in which to be forgotten. The foothill skyline bounded their view of life there. A man with vision beyond that skyline came to them, Connor promises. By sheer love and faith he won them to believe life is priceless. The contents then begin with the foothills country and the company of the noble seven.
the-social-emergency-studies-in-sex-hygi: William Trufant Foster edited The Social Emergency, studies in sex hygiene and morals. Foster was president of Reed College. Charles W. Eliot, president emeritus of Harvard, supplied an introduction. Houghton Mifflin held the 1914 copyright. The pages shown give the title matter and the start of the contents only. Eliot's introduction comes first, at page one. Foster's own essay on the social emergency follows. Arthur Evans Wood handles economic phases at page forty-five. No essay text itself appears here.
the-story-of-a-lamb-on-wheels:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this Make Believe story in ten chapters. It follows a toy lamb. The lamb meets a jolly sailor. She slides downhill and falls down a coal hole. She sails down a brook toward Mirabell's happiness. Chapter one, The Lamb's Wish, opens inside a toy store as the Jack in the Box pops his head out.

The Jack's black fringe of whiskers jiggles as his big eyes look around and he cries hurray that the toys are alone at last and can have some fun. That nightly waking of the toys launches the Lamb on Wheels into the small dangers and rescues that fill Hope's department-store world for young readers.
the-story-of-the-two-bulls:
A verse tale printed with original engravings by Daniel Burgess and Company of New York in 1856, with no author's name on the pages present here, tells of Deacon R., neither the worst man in the world nor the best by far. His fields were rich and his acres broad. Cattle were his pride: oxen, sheep, and horses beside.

The poem lingers over his prize brindle cow. She stood highest at the county fair. It lingers over Old Bonny Gray too. The steed was noble and famous at the race before the deacon bought him. The deacon would tell that story. Then he would sigh that such sports are far from right. Still more than all, a spotted bull filled the deacon's mind, until a neighbour, Moses Grimes, enters the tale.
the-tale-of-pony-twinkleheels: Arthur Scott Bailey's Pony Twinkleheels, a Slumber-Town Tale, was published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1921, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. Barely more than the title leaf is present in this record, naming the book, its series, and Bailey's Sleepy-Time and Tuck-Me-In collections. A frontispiece note mentions Twinkleheels racing with Ebenezer, which suggests pony contests ahead. No chapters and no opening scene appear, so the little pony's story cannot be read or fairly summarized from what is shown here.
the-two-vanrevels:
Booth Tarkington opens his novel in a mellow, candlelit age of dancing and romance. Old Carewe drives home from a convent with his lovely daughter Betty, her harp strapped behind the carriage and farewell bouquets piled around her. Betty's arrival in Rouen sets young hearts at risk from the first chapter.

Playful chapter titles promise political quarrels, a serenade, a room in a cupola, a silenced witness, and a flag marching by. Later headings name the firm of Gray and Vanrevel, hinting at business rivalry alongside courtship. Readers get a period love story told with humour, local colour, and a strong sense of a vanished, more romantic time.
the-wonderful-adventures-of-nils: Selma Lagerlöf's The Wonderful Adventures of Nils is presented here by its contents list alone. Velma Swanston Howard translated the book from the Swedish. Chapters follow Nils, Akka from Kebnekaise, and a wonderful journey. Places named include Glimminge Castle, Karlskrona, and Öland. A legend of Småland and a story of crows appear. The adventure chapters themselves do not appear in these pages.
tom-tufton-s-travels:
Evelyn Everett-Green's story opens with Squire Tufton of Gablehurst dying slowly, his strong figure wasted to a shadow. Contents list fifteen chapters following his only son out into the world, into gay London town, and into folly with Lord Claud. Master Gale's daughter and the great duke enter the tale.

The squire's wife and daughter nurse him in turns, sharing neither his certainty nor the household's returning hope of recovery. Later headings promise peril, pious monks of St. Bernard, the king's highway, and a forest flight. Readers get a historical family story beginning at a deathbed.
two-festivals:
Mrs. Follen's Two Festivals collects three pieces for children: May Morning and New Year's Eve, The Birthday, and A True Story. Illustrations by Billings and others accompany the tales. The first story opens on the evening before May Day in the Chilton household.

Mrs. Chilton reads Milton's lines on the bright morning star aloud to Frank and Harry. The younger boy fears rain, hail, or snow will spoil the woods party, the wreath for Lizzy Evans as May queen, and the dinner in the woods. His mother counsels enjoying May morning with the mind's eye, as the blind poet did. Ned Brown's flageolet and a dance after tea hang on the weather.
un-doc-protocol-to-the-agreement-on-the-:
Books, lab gear, and works of art cross borders more easily under this protocol, which extends a 1950 United Nations agreement on the import of educational, scientific, and cultural materials. The parent pact cut customs duties on goods that spread learning and culture. The protocol widens and updates that promise.

The text lists the kinds of materials that states agree to admit with fewer barriers. It reflects a postwar belief that free flows of books and tools help peace and progress. For readers, it shows trade law being used in the service of schools, labs, and museums.
uncle-wiggily-s-travels: Uncle Wiggily's Travels, by Howard R. Garis and illustrated by Louis Wisa, was published by A. L. Burt in 1913. Its opening pages repeat the Bed Time Series advertisement: thirty-one stories a volume, one for each night of the month. Garis's name also stands behind the Island Boys and Those Smith Boys series. Only the title page and series advertisements are present here, so the rabbit's travels themselves do not appear.
villehardouin-conquest-constantinople-ma:
Geoffroi de Villehardouin, a French knight and marshal of Champagne, wrote The Conquest of Constantinople around 1213. Frank T. Marzials's English translation is the text here. The work is the earliest surviving chronicle in French prose, and its author helped make the events he tells.

Villehardouin recounts the Fourth Crusade from inside the leadership: the treaty with Venice, the swerve to Zara, and the diversion to Constantinople. The great city falls twice, in 1203 and 1204, and a Latin empire is set on its throne. His telling is proud and partial, a commander's defense of a scandalous crusade. No closer witness survives.
vocational-guidance-for-girls: Marguerite Stockman Dickson wrote Vocational Guidance for Girls. Rand McNally and Company issued it at Chicago and New York. Pages present here hold an advertisement for other books in the same series, a photograph of Camp Fire Girls, and the title page. The guidance itself is not shown. The photograph's caption praises the Camp Fire Girls for lessons in patriotism, kindness, and industry. Dickson's other works, named on the title page, run from tales of the old world to stories of camp and trail.
while-the-billy-boils: The pages here hold just the title page and a contents list for Henry Lawson's While the Billy Boils, so his tales do not appear. A note flags a name slip in one tale, present since the first edition. The contents list a first series of bush tales. Titles include An Old Mate of Your Father's, Settling on the Land, and Enter Mitchell. Hungerford, A Camp-fire Yarn, and The Union Buries Its Dead follow. The list sketches Lawson's world of swagmen and dry plains.
wholesale-price-list-of-newspapers-and-p: The pages here hold a transcriber's note and the cover of a 1905 subscription catalog, with none of the price lists themselves shown. D. D. Cottrell ran a subscription agency at North Cohocton, New York, from 1886. His catalog number 39 offered wholesale prices on newspapers and periodicals. The note warns that the offers are long dead and most of the titles have ceased. The booklet ran to forty pages, with club offers that paired titles at special prices. Cottrell, the note adds, loved horseshoe pitching.
with-edged-tools: Only the title page and contents are present here for Henry Seton Merriman's With Edged Tools, so the novel itself does not appear. Merriman gave the book to James Payn as a token of regard. A Bible verse on the potter and his vessels heads the work. The contents open with two generations and a farewell. A tragedy, the secret of the Simiacine, and a place called Loango follow. War, ivory, and consignments fill the middle list. Nemesis, a rescue, and peril close the titles shown.
